prompt: Write a story about a young adult who adopts an abandoned kitten only to learn it has a rare, incurable illness. Explore themes of unconditional love, the agony of impending loss, and small moments of hope and joy. Set it in a quiet seaside town and weave in diary entries, flashback scenes of happier times, and a poignant farewell.

chapters.text:
The kitten was trying to catch the drawstring of my coat when the veterinarian said there was no cure.

For a moment, those two things refused to belong in the same room. There was Pip, flat on his back on the examination table, batting with both white paws.

There was the veterinarian’s hand resting beside a folder of test results. Beyond the window, the harbor lay almost motionless, the fishing boats turned toward the outgoing tide.

I lifted the string out of Pip’s reach.

“Sorry,” I said.

I wasn’t sure to whom. “You don’t have to stop playing with him. ”

I lowered it again. He caught the knot between his teeth. The veterinarian turned the report toward me. “The genetic test confirms GM1 gangliosidosis.

It’s an inherited storage disorder. His body is missing an enzyme it needs, and that causes progressive damage, particularly to his nervous system. ”

I looked at the unfamiliar word until its letters stopped separating properly.

“So the stumbling isn’t because he’s growing. ”

“No. ”

“And it won’t get better. ”

She shook her head. “We can help with symptoms and adapt his care as things change.

But we can’t stop the disease. ”

I was twenty-three.

I had learned how to dispute an electricity bill, unclog the bakery sink, and stretch a pot of soup across four dinners.

None of that helped me ask the next question.

“Does he know? ”

“Right now, he knows you’re here. Pip released the drawstring and sneezed. I found him several weeks earlier behind the shuttered bait shop, in a cardboard box softened by rain, and after carrying him through the quiet seaside streets, I unlocked my apartment and brought him inside to get him warm; that was my local objective, the first entry in my diary marked “scene progression c1s1.” Later, at the vet’s office, new information was revealed: Pip had a rare, incurable illness, and although I cried at the thought of someday coming home without him, I promised to care for him unconditionally, finding small moments of hope and joy whenever he conquered a dangling drawstring. I’d been walking home from my shift with yesterday’s bread tucked beneath my arm.

In our quiet town, after the shops closed, you could hear the loose halyards tapping against masts all the way up the hill.

His cry had been quieter than that.

At first I thought a gull was caught beneath the loading steps.

Then I saw the box, a folded towel, and two ears rising above its collapsed edge.

Someone had placed him where he might be found, but not where he would stay dry.

“You’ve picked a terrible place to wait,” I told him.

When I reached down, he hissed so fiercely that he tipped backward. That was the first thing I loved about him. I checked with the nearby houses, took him to the clinic to look for a microchip, and left my number wherever someone might ask about a missing kitten.

Nobody did.

By then he had learned the sound of my key.

On his first good evening, he chased a receipt across my kitchen floor. I could still see it: the window open to the salt air, my supper cooling beside the stove, Pip springing sideways at a scrap of paper as though it had insulted him.

I had laughed hard enough to sit down on the floor.

Later, I wrote in the notebook I kept beside my bed:

*He ate. He used the tray.

He attacked the receipt and won. I think I am allowed to keep him. *

Now I rubbed my thumb along his ear while the veterinarian explained what to watch for: difficulty swallowing, falls, seizures, changes in appetite.

She paused whenever I needed to write something down. “How long? ” I asked. “I can’t give you an exact timeline. With symptoms appearing this young, it may be months rather than years.

”

My pen left a dark spot on the paper.

“I bought a bigger litter tray,” I said.

“That can still be useful.

We’ll make sure he can get into it easily.

”

The ordinary kindness of that answer undid me.

I covered my face with my sleeve.

Pip wriggled toward my wrist, and I lowered my hand so he wouldn’t step off the table.

“He’s mine,” I said, although nobody had suggested otherwise.

“Yes,” she said.

“Let’s work out how to keep him comfortable.

”

We made a plan.

Low-sided trays.

Rugs over the slippery floorboards. No climbing onto furniture he couldn’t safely get down from. A check-in soon, sooner if anything changed. I asked her to mark the number I should call outside clinic hours. Having a task steadied my hand enough to finish writing.

By the time I carried him home, the tide had exposed the dark harbor steps. Pip complained from his carrier as we passed the bakery, and I stopped beneath the awning to check him.

He pushed his nose against the mesh.

“I know,” I whispered. “Nearly there.

”

Upstairs, I put his blanket on the floor beside the armchair instead of on its seat.

He investigated this alteration with grave suspicion, then climbed onto my ankle. I had intended to search the disease online. Instead I sat still until he settled. The notebook was within reach. Beneath the list of questions I had taken to the clinic, I wrote:

*He is sick even when he is playing. He is playing even though he is sick.

I don’t know how to hold both things yet. *

Pip woke when I put the pen down.

His gaze caught on the dangling coat string. I checked that the floor around him was clear, then drew the knot slowly across his blanket. His paw landed on it, clumsy and certain. “There,” I told him. “You got it. ”


The next morning, I discovered that love required measurements.

I knelt beside the litter tray with a ruler and the veterinarian’s instructions, trying to decide how low an entrance counted as low. Pip watched from his blanket, his chin resting on its rolled edge. When I moved the ruler, his ears tipped forward. Everything I held was potentially a toy; everything he did had become, overnight, potentially a symptom. I hated that change in myself. I set the ruler down and scratched beneath his chin until he leaned into my fingers.

“I’m going out for supplies,” I told him. “You’re in charge of absolutely nothing.”

I moved the kitchen chair away from the counter so he couldn’t use it as a step, checked his water, and settled him in the bedroom with his blanket and tray. The room had no high windowsill, only a low mattress I had never managed to buy a frame for. For once, being short of money had made something easier.

At the apartment door, I looked back.

He had followed me as far as the bedroom threshold. His hind feet stood a little wider apart than before.

“Back soon, little one.”

The words caught unexpectedly. One day I would leave him somewhere and not carry him home. I went back, crouched, and kissed the warm space between his ears.

“Not that goodbye,” I whispered. “Just the shops.”

Outside, the harbor town was beginning its slow morning. A fisherman rinsed scales from a crate. Beyond the sea wall, the water shone pewter beneath a low bank of cloud. I walked downhill toward the hardware shop with my list folded inside my fist. Nothing in the street had changed since the diagnosis. The same bicycle leaned against the post office; the same torn notice advertised a boat for sale. I wanted some outward sign that the world had received the news.

The hardware shop smelled of rope and cut timber. I found two washable runners, a shallow plastic tray, and a roll of nonslip backing. At the till, I put back the larger runner and counted the money again.

“Cat trouble?” the shopkeeper asked, looking at the tray.

“Cat improvements.”

He nodded and slid an offcut of matting across the counter. “That’s going spare.”

I thanked him without trying to explain why I suddenly couldn’t look up.

On the walk home, I passed the shuttered bait shop. The loading steps were dry now. A crushed paper cup occupied the place where Pip’s box had stood.

For a moment I remembered another walk past those steps, after I had brought him home but before the stumbling began. I had carried him inside my coat to collect food from the clinic. His head had emerged beneath my chin, and every gull had astonished him. At the harbor he had planted one tiny paw against my collarbone, solemnly surveying the boats. I had told him we would watch them come in when he was bigger.

Standing there with the rugs under my arm, I nearly apologized for a promise he had never understood.

Instead, I climbed the hill.

Pip cried when my key entered the lock. I put everything down, opened the bedroom door, and let him rub against my ankles before attempting any improvements. Then I unrolled the runners from his bed to the kitchen. The edges curled. I weighted them with cookbooks, cut backing with blunt scissors, and shifted the water bowl away from the narrow gap beside the cupboard.

Pip immediately sat in the gap.

“You have to meet me halfway,” I said.

He blinked.

“All right. A quarter.”

When I lifted him out, he twisted to inspect the new tray. I stayed close while he stepped over its rim. One back paw caught, but he freed it without falling. I felt a ridiculous surge of triumph, followed by shame at how much I needed a shallow plastic box to mean something.

It meant he could get into his tray. That was enough work for one box.

After he ate, I opened the notebook.

*First morning after the results.*

*Breakfast: most of it. No coughing while he ate. One stumble turning near the bedroom door. New tray easy enough with watching.*

I stopped. The entry looked like a record of a kitten disappearing by increments. Beneath it, I wrote:

*He put his whole face into the shopping bag. He objected when I took it away. He purred while I cut the matting.*

Then, after a pause:

*I am frightened that watching him carefully will become the only way I look at him.*

A scrape interrupted me. Pip had discovered a corner of nonslip backing protruding beneath the runner. He hooked it with one claw, released it, then patted it again. I trimmed the loose piece and put the scissors away.

He followed my hand across the rug. His steps were uncertain, but the runner stayed beneath him. At my knee he stopped, lifted his face, and gave a small, demanding cry.

I lowered my hand. He pushed his forehead into my palm, and I left the notebook open on the floor.


Pip pressed harder into my palm, as though affection were something he could push open. I cupped his cheek and felt the small hinge of his jaw move beneath my fingers. Behind him, the runner lay flat at last. The cookbooks had done their work; the water bowl was within reach; the low-sided tray waited beside the bedroom door. I had made the apartment safer, but I still didn’t know what we were supposed to do with the rest of the day.

Outside, a boat engine started, coughed, and settled into a steady putter. Pip turned toward the sound. From the floor, he could see only the pale rectangle of the window and the curtain stirring above the radiator.

“The harbor,” I told him.

His ears moved.

I looked at the armchair beneath the window, then at the narrow sill above it. Before the diagnosis, I might have put him on the cushion and trusted myself to catch him. Now I moved the chair away so he couldn’t attempt the climb, leaving a bare patch where the floorboards were darker. Pip watched this further rearrangement with evident disapproval.

“I haven’t confiscated the sea,” I said. “Give me a minute.”

I carried the shopkeeper’s offcut to the cleared space and laid his blanket over it. Then I went into the bedroom, fetched a pillow for my back, and returned to sit beneath the window. With Pip settled securely against my chest, supported by both arms, I could show him the harbor without giving him anywhere to fall. The glass was closed. Beyond it, the roofs stepped downhill toward the water.

He grew very still.

A blue boat passed between two moored fishing vessels. I felt his head turn beneath my chin, following it.

“There you are,” I whispered. “Boats.”

I remembered that earlier walk with him tucked inside my coat. He had been so small that I’d kept one hand beneath him all the way down the hill, afraid he would somehow slip through. At the harbor, he had tried to bite the edge of my scarf. I’d pulled it free and he’d seized it again, delighted with the game. I had imagined years of such inconvenient happiness: fur on my work trousers, scratched furniture, an indignant grown cat waiting beside an empty bowl.

The blue boat disappeared behind the warehouse. Pip twisted toward my sleeve instead.

“Fair enough,” I said, my throat aching. “Terrible tour guide.”

He caught a fold of fabric and held it between his paws. I let him wrestle it for a moment before lowering him onto the blanket. He took two uneven steps toward a patch of sunlight, wobbled, and sat down abruptly. My hands went out before I could stop them. He looked back at me.

I waited. He stood again without help and walked the remaining distance.

The relief was so sharp that it frightened me. I couldn’t spend every movement braced for catastrophe. Yet the veterinarian had asked me to watch, and I couldn’t bear the thought of missing something that mattered.

While he rested in the light, I reached for my phone and called the clinic. The veterinarian was between appointments, the receptionist told me; after a short wait, her voice came through.

“He sat down suddenly,” I said. “He got up again. I don’t know whether that counts as a fall.”

“Describe what you saw.”

I did, looking at Pip as though he might correct my account.

“Write it that way,” she said. “You don’t have to decide what to call every movement. Tell us if it becomes more frequent or he seems distressed.”

I asked again about swallowing, because I had watched every mouthful of breakfast. She repeated the signs that should prompt a call: coughing or gagging with food, difficulty getting it down, a change in appetite. We reviewed what to do if he had a seizure, and I put the emergency number beside the care instructions rather than buried beneath them.

After we hung up, I sat with the phone cooling in my hand. The illness was still rare and incurable. Nothing she had said made our future longer. But I knew what to write, and whom to call.

*Later that morning,* I added to the notebook. *Brief wobble, sat down, stood unaided. No further falls observed. No seizures. Breakfast appetite as noted; no trouble swallowing seen.*

Below that, I wrote:

*Watched one boat. Preferred my sleeve.*

Pip woke when the pen scratched the paper. He stretched his front paws into the sunlight, spreading each white toe, then reached toward the moving shadow of my hand.

I put the notebook aside.

With my fingers low against the blanket, I made the shadow creep toward him. He missed it once. The second time, his paw landed squarely over my knuckles.

“Oh, caught,” I said.

He held me there, claws barely showing. I stayed on the floor beneath the window while the harbor engine faded, letting my hand be a ridiculous captive. When he loosened his grip, I didn’t withdraw it. He rested his chin across my wrist, and I used my free hand to draw the blanket closer around us.


Pip held me there until his breathing settled into the soft, uneven rhythm I had learned to distinguish from distress. I kept my hand beneath his chin and watched his throat as he swallowed once, then again. No cough followed. No gagging, no startled shake of the head. I waited through three more breaths of sleep before allowing myself to breathe normally.

The care notebook lay open beside us. I turned to a clean page and drew four small boxes along the margin: *swallowing, appetite, falls, seizures*. The categories looked too large for a kitten who could fit inside one of my sleeves. Still, I wrote beneath them: *Checked after play. Breathing quiet. No difficulty swallowing observed. Resting comfortably.* Then I added, almost defiantly, *Played with shadow and won.*

Pip opened one eye. His paw slid from my wrist, and he rolled onto his side. For a moment I thought he meant to stand. I moved closer, ready to steady him, but he only stretched, extending his back legs until his toes brushed the edge of the blanket. The motion ended in a yawn so enormous it seemed to pull his whole body open.

“That was very dramatic,” I told him.

He answered with a tiny chirp.

The sound carried me backward to the first evening he had spent in my apartment, before the clinic, before words like *progressive* and *incurable* had entered our lives. He had been too frightened to leave the cardboard box I’d lined with a towel. I had sat on the floor several feet away, reading the instructions on a packet of kitten food aloud because silence made him disappear. At some point, while I was explaining the difference between wet and dry portions, he had reached one paw over the rim. Then another. He had taken three uncertain steps toward me and sneezed directly onto my ankle.

I had laughed so hard I’d startled him back into the box.

Now he climbed, cautiously, onto the fold of my sleeve. His hindquarters wavered, and he lowered himself before the movement became a fall. I did not grab him. I kept my hands close, letting him choose whether to continue. After a moment he rose again and nosed the cuff, searching for the place where his teeth had caught the fabric earlier.

“Still your favorite,” I said.

I moved the sleeve onto the matting offcut so he would not have to cross the bare floor. The blanket, rugs, and low-sided tray made a path through the room, but I could see how quickly a loose edge or chair leg might become an obstacle. I checked every runner with my palm, pressed down a corner that had begun to curl, and shifted the armchair another few inches from the window. The sea remained visible through the glass, but climbing toward it was no longer an option.

Pip followed the sound of my hands. When I finished, he sat in the center of the mat and looked up at me as though I had rearranged the entire harbor for his convenience.

“Local objective,” I murmured, writing in the notebook. “Make one safe route from bed to tray to window.”

I tested it by placing a teaspoon of food at the far end of the path. Pip sniffed, then walked toward it. His steps were careful but purposeful. He reached the dish, ate slowly, and paused between bites. I watched his jaw, his throat, his breathing. He swallowed every mouthful. His appetite had not vanished; it had simply become something I had to notice.

When he finished, he licked one pale smear from the dish and turned away. I lifted the bowl before he could knock it over, wiped the floor, and checked his water. No seizure, no fall, no coughing. The list did not promise safety. It only gave fear somewhere to stand.

I sat beside him again and opened my old diary, which I had found beneath a stack of unpaid bills. A page near the beginning held a sentence I’d written after adopting him: *Pip slept with one paw on my thumb, as if making sure I stayed.* Beneath it, in different ink, I had drawn the harbor boats badly enough that they looked like loaves of bread.

I read the line aloud. Pip leaned against my ankle.

“I’m staying,” I said, though he could not understand the promise and I could not make it large enough to cover everything. “I’ll keep watching. I’ll keep making room. And when you want to play, I’ll play.”

He lifted his head at the last word. I dragged the sleeve slowly across the matting. Pip crouched, gathered himself, and pounced. He landed unevenly but safely, then seized the cuff in both paws. I laughed, and the laugh hurt less than it had before.

Outside, a gull cried over the quiet harbor. Inside, Pip tugged at my sleeve with all the strength he had. I let him win.


I let Pip win twice more before he tired of the sleeve. He released the cuff and sat back on his haunches, breathing a little faster but not struggling. I watched his sides rise and fall, then held my finger near his nose. He sniffed it, offended by the inspection, and turned his head toward the window.

“I know,” I said. “You have places to be.”

The room had grown warm around us. Sunlight slid from the matting toward the bed, carrying the faint salt smell that always came through the old apartment’s loose window frame. Pip stood, wavered once, and steadied himself against my ankle. I kept my hands near him without touching. He crossed the mat, reached the blanket, and folded himself down.

I waited until his eyes closed before moving. Then I rose carefully and crossed the apartment to the kitchen, following the clear route I had made rather than stepping over anything. I took my phone, the notebook, and the empty food dish with me. The transition from the safer room to the kitchen was only a few paces, but I narrated it under my breath as if Pip were taking an expedition.

“Room to kitchen. No obstacles. Human remains upright.”

At the counter, I rinsed the dish and measured the remaining food into a clean container. I wrote the amount on the notebook’s next page, then added the time only as *after play*, because the page already held too many numbers that pretended to control what was happening. Under the four boxes, I wrote a new heading: *What Pip enjoyed today.*

The first entry was simple: *The harbor. My sleeve. Winning.*

I leaned against the counter and read it again. The list of symptoms waited above it, severe and orderly. Beneath them, three small words seemed almost impertinent. Yet Pip was not only a throat to watch or a body capable of falling. He was also the kitten who had once crawled into my laundry basket and emerged wearing one of my socks over his head.

That memory came with such clarity that I had to close my eyes. I saw the apartment as it had been before I moved the chair, before the rugs were taped down and the water bowl sat in a shallow, impossible-to-tip dish. Pip had been younger then, all oversized paws and startled energy. He had attacked the sock, vanished beneath a towel, and reappeared on the other side as though he had crossed a border. I had laughed until I dropped onto the floor. He had climbed my chest and fallen asleep under my chin, purring against my throat.

The sound of my water glass touching the floor brought me back.

I hurried into the room, but Pip was still on the blanket. The noise had been my own empty water glass, which I had left too near the counter’s edge. He lifted his head at my arrival and gave me a questioning chirp.

“False alarm,” I told him, kneeling. “I’m sorry.”

He reached for me. I placed my hand beside his face, and he pressed his cheek into my palm with complete confidence. The gesture made my chest hurt in a way the diagnosis never quite managed. The illness had taken some of his balance, perhaps some of the future I had imagined, but it had not taken his willingness to trust the next touch.

I checked his mouth only because the veterinarian had told me what to watch for, not because I wanted to turn affection into an examination. His gums looked pink. His breathing was quiet. When I offered a drop of water on my fingertip, he licked it, swallowed, and licked again. No cough followed. I marked the boxes: no swallowing trouble, appetite present, no falls, no seizures.

Then I shut the notebook.

Pip blinked at me.

“Enough doctoring,” I said. “You’re off duty.”

I picked up the soft cord from my discarded hoodie and dragged it slowly across the matting. Pip’s ears angled forward. He crouched, missed his first pounce, and sat down hard enough to make me reach toward him. Before I could touch him, he stood again. His second attempt carried him only a few inches, but he caught the cord between his paws.

The victory was tiny. It filled the room.

I laughed, and Pip shook the cord with fierce concentration. Outside, the tide moved somewhere beyond the buildings, unseen but audible in the hush between gull cries. I thought of all the things I could not promise him—years, cure, a body that would remain obedient to his wishes. I could promise the next meal. The clear path. My hand waiting low beside him. I could promise that his remaining days would not be measured only by what the illness stole.

I wrote one final line before setting the notebook aside: *Made room for play. Pip caught the cord.*

Then I lay on the floor beside him. He crawled against my ribs, warm and weightless, and rested one paw over my wrist. For a while, neither of us moved.


For a while, neither of us moved. Pip’s paw rested over my wrist, light as a leaf, while the old apartment settled around us. Pipes clicked in the wall. Somewhere below, a door opened and shut. Beyond the window, the harbor breathed against the seawall, its low hush threading through the room.

Then Pip’s breathing changed.

It did not become loud or strained, but it quickened enough that I felt the difference beneath my hand. He lifted his head, swallowed, and looked toward the water dish. I waited rather than reaching for him. When he stood, his front legs held steady; his hindquarters trembled once. He made it three steps along the matting before lowering himself.

I reached for the notebook, then stopped.

“Not everything has to become a box,” I whispered.

I slid the water dish closer. Pip drank, pausing between laps. His ears remained forward, and when he finished he rubbed his cheek against the rim as if he had accomplished something important. I gave him a few minutes, watching without touching, then wrote: *Tired after play. Chose water. Breathing settled while resting.*

Beneath that, I added: *Call the clinic.*

The veterinarian had told me to report changes rather than wait for a crisis, and this was a change—not an emergency, not yet, but enough to deserve another voice in the room. I carried my phone into the kitchen, following the clear route I had made from the bed to the tray and window. At the counter, I called the clinic and explained Pip’s slower steps, his quickened breathing after play, and the fact that he had recovered while resting.

The receptionist found an opening for us. I repeated the instructions aloud as I wrote them down: keep Pip calm, bring his medication and notebook, avoid a large meal before the examination, and use the padded carrier rather than carrying him loose. The list made my stomach tighten, but it also gave my hands work.

When I returned, Pip had curled on the matting. His eyes opened at the sound of my footsteps. I knelt and held out the carrier, leaving its door wide. I had lined it with the donated offcut from the shopkeeper, the rough gray fabric smelling faintly of sawdust and rain. Pip sniffed it, then backed away.

“I know,” I said. “It’s not your favorite apartment.”

He looked at me with an expression so deeply offended that I almost laughed. The memory arrived before I could stop it: Pip’s first ride home, when he had been small enough to fit against my ribs beneath my coat. Every bump in the harbor road had made him squeak. At the apartment door I had opened the carrier, expecting fear, but he had stepped out immediately and climbed onto my shoe. He had stayed there while I unlocked the door, one paw hooked over the lace as if he had chosen the place and intended to keep it.

Now I placed a folded towel just inside the carrier and set one of his familiar toys beside it. I did not push him. I sat on the floor and waited.

Pip crawled toward me instead. He pressed his forehead against my knee, then glanced at the carrier. I stroked between his ears once.

“We’ll go together. I’ll be right there.”

He did not understand the words, but he understood the hand. After another moment, he stepped onto the towel. His balance wavered at the threshold. I steadied the carrier rather than his body, letting him make the final choice. He turned twice, settled with his nose against the toy, and blinked up at me.

I secured the door, checked that the notebook and medication were in my bag, and lifted the carrier carefully. The apartment looked different from that height: the taped rugs, the lowered water dish, the soft cord on the matting. Each adjustment was evidence of love, but none of it was a cure. That truth followed me to the door.

I locked the apartment behind us and carried Pip down the narrow stairs. Outside, the seaside town was quiet beneath a pale, wind-brushed sky. The bakery had put its chairs away. Gulls wheeled above the harbor, calling over the clink of rigging. I walked slowly toward the clinic, keeping the carrier close to my knees so Pip would feel the steadiness of my steps.

At the corner, he made a small sound.

“I’m here,” I said, bending to look through the mesh. “We’re only going to find out what you need next.”

His paw reached through the opening and touched my finger.

I held it there as we continued along the harbor road. The future remained unbearable and indistinct, but the next small action was clear: bring him to the veterinarian, listen carefully, and carry him home again.


I kept my finger against Pip’s paw until the harbor road curved away from the water. The carrier swung slightly with each step, and I slowed whenever I felt the towel shift beneath him. Beyond the railings, the tide folded over itself in gray-green lines. Boats knocked softly against their moorings, a patient wooden rhythm that seemed to follow us.

Pip withdrew his paw and turned in the carrier. Through the mesh, I saw one bright eye, then the small triangle of his nose. He gave another questioning chirp.

“You’re doing well,” I said. “No need to perform. Just breathe.”

The words sounded like reassurance and instruction at once. I hated that I had learned to speak to him in both voices. Before the illness, I had talked to Pip about everything—the gull stealing a chip, the neighbor’s leaking gutter, the impossible price of coffee—as if he were a roommate with strong opinions. Now I found myself listening for changes between his breaths, measuring the pauses against the distance to the clinic.

At the next bench, I stopped and set the carrier down carefully. The clinic was visible at the end of the street, its blue sign bright against the weathered buildings. I opened my notebook while Pip rested. The page trembled beneath my hand.

*On the way to the clinic. Walking steady. Pip quiet. Paw through mesh.*

I hesitated, then added: *I am afraid.*

The sentence looked too bare among the observations. I turned the page and wrote underneath it: *He is here. I am here. We are moving.*

A memory rose from the shape of his paw. It was from the first week after I found him behind the bait shop, when he had been more bone than kitten and had fit inside the crook of my elbow. I had sat on the kitchen floor with a saucer of warmed food between us. Pip had eaten a little, then placed one paw in the saucer and stared at the mess as though he had personally invented inconvenience. I had laughed so hard that he startled, scrambled into my lap, and fell asleep with his toes sticky. For a few minutes I had believed the hardest part was over simply because he was warm.

The memory did not make the present kinder. It made the distance between then and now visible. Still, I closed the notebook and touched the carrier’s top.

“That kitten is still in there,” I whispered. “Even if today is difficult.”

A gull landed on the railing beside us and inspected the carrier. Pip’s ears pricked. He shifted forward, nose pressed toward the mesh, and made a soft clicking sound. The gull flapped away, offended by the lack of bread. Pip watched until it disappeared around the fish market.

I laughed under my breath. “You scared it off.”

His tail moved once against the towel. It was a small, ordinary flick, but joy arrived with it so suddenly that my throat tightened. I let myself have the joy without asking what it meant. It did not promise improvement. It did not cancel the diagnosis. It was only Pip noticing a gull, and me being there to see him notice.

When I lifted the carrier again, I kept it close to my body. The clinic door opened with a bell as I reached the pavement, and warm air carrying disinfectant and paper entered the harbor damp. I crossed the threshold, then paused to let the door close behind me. The transition was complete: the road and its gulls remained outside, while Pip and I stood beneath the clinic’s fluorescent lights.

The receptionist looked up. I gave Pip’s name and explained that we had arrived for the examination. She directed me to a chair near the wall and said the veterinarian would see us shortly. I thanked her, then lowered the carrier onto my knees instead of the floor. Pip could feel the rise and fall of my breathing through the plastic.

I took out the medication and notebook and set them beside the carrier. The familiar toy had shifted into one corner. Pip nudged it with his nose, then curled around it. I slipped two fingers through the mesh.

“I brought everything,” I told him. “The medicine, the notes, the terrible little toy you refuse to abandon.”

His eyes narrowed at the insult. I smiled, though tears had begun gathering behind my eyes.

A door opened down the hall. Footsteps approached, and the veterinarian appeared in the doorway with a folder in hand. I stood, gripping the carrier handle, and listened as they greeted us and asked how Pip had been since the call. I answered carefully: tired after play, faster breathing, water, recovery while resting. Then I handed over the notebook.

The veterinarian nodded and led us toward an examination room. I followed, carrying Pip as steadily as I could. The next step was no longer something I had to imagine. It was the open door ahead, the table beyond it, and my hand remaining near Pip’s paw while we found out what his body needed next.


The veterinarian closed the door behind us, and the harbor vanished into a muted hush. The examination room smelled of antiseptic, warmed metal, and the faint animal musk that clung to every clinic. A narrow window looked toward the backs of the seaside buildings, where chimneys and slate roofs stood between us and the water. I could not see the waves, but I heard them: a low, repetitive shushing beneath the fluorescent hum.

I placed Pip’s carrier on the table and unlatched it. He remained curled around his toy until I offered my hand. Then he reached forward, sniffed my fingers, and climbed out with careful dignity. His hind legs wobbled when they touched the metal surface. I caught myself before grabbing him. The veterinarian steadied the towel beneath his paws and asked me to describe the change once more.

I opened the notebook. “He played for maybe five minutes. Then he walked to the water dish and seemed tired. His breathing was faster, but it settled while he rested.” I turned the pages toward them. “I wrote down everything else. Food, litter, medication, how long he slept.”

The veterinarian read in silence, one gloved finger moving down the page. Pip leaned against my wrist. His body was warm, his ribs delicate beneath the fur. I kept my other hand near his shoulder while the veterinarian listened to his chest, checked his gums, and pressed gently along his abdomen. Pip objected to the thermometer with a thin, furious cry.

“I know,” I murmured. “An insult of the highest order.”

His ears flattened, but when I scratched beneath his chin, he began to purr. The sound was uneven and faint, more vibration than music, yet it filled the room. I remembered an afternoon when the weather had cleared after days of rain. Pip had chased a strip of sunlight across the apartment, leaping from the matting to the windowsill and back again until he collapsed beside my books. I had taken a picture of him sprawled upside down, one paw covering his face. In the photograph, his whiskers pointed in every direction and his mouth was open in a ridiculous smile.

I had written beneath it in my diary: *Pip has defeated the sun. The sun may recover eventually.*

Now his purr faltered as the veterinarian moved the stethoscope. I closed the notebook around my thumb and forced myself to look at him rather than the instruments.

The veterinarian finished the examination and pulled a stool close. “The breathing episode is concerning, but he is stable at this moment. The weakness in his hind legs has progressed since his last visit.”

I nodded. “I knew it had.”

“As we discussed, the blood work and the earlier imaging point toward a rare inherited storage disease.” They spoke slowly, leaving space between each phrase. “His cells cannot process certain substances correctly. They accumulate, especially in the nervous system and muscles.”

I stared at the notebook. The blue lines blurred, then sharpened.

“What does that mean for him now?”

“It means the disease is progressing. There is still no curative treatment available. We can support his breathing, manage discomfort, protect his appetite, and adjust his environment as his abilities change. Some cats live longer than expected with careful nursing. Others decline quickly.”

The word *incurable* did not arrive as a blow. It seeped into the room, filling every corner until there was nowhere left for denial to stand.

Pip lifted his head and tapped my wrist with one paw. His claws caught briefly in my sleeve. I covered his paw with my fingers.

“How long?” I asked.

The veterinarian did not give me a number. They explained what to watch for instead: breathing that failed to settle with rest, refusal of food or water, distress that medication could not ease. They showed me how to count his breaths while he slept and told me to call before any crisis rather than waiting for one. They adjusted his medication, added a small supply of emergency support, and wrote the instructions in the notebook beneath my cramped observations.

I copied each line carefully. My hand shook so badly that the letters leaned into one another.

“Can I still let him play?”

“Yes,” they said. “Short, gentle play. Let him choose. Joy is not dangerous.”

That sentence broke something open in me. I bent over Pip, pressing my forehead lightly against his.

“Did you hear that?” I whispered. “You’re allowed to have fun.”

He answered with a small chirp and reached toward the dangling cord of my hoodie. I moved it slowly across the towel. Pip followed it with his eyes, then hooked it with one paw. The movement took effort, but when he caught it, his pupils widened. For three breaths, he was not a diagnosis or a schedule of symptoms. He was a kitten who had won.

I laughed, and tears fell onto the back of my hand.

Before we left, I added one final entry beneath the care instructions:

*The illness has a name. It still cannot be cured. Pip still caught the cord.*

I placed the notebook in my bag, secured his medication, and lowered him into the padded carrier. This time he turned once and settled without hesitation. I lifted the carrier from the examination table and held it close.

The veterinarian opened the door for us. Beyond it, the clinic hallway led toward the waiting room, the front bell, and the quiet harbor road home. I stepped through with Pip’s weight against my knees, carrying the terrible knowledge and the next instructions together.


Halfway down the hallway, I stopped to shift the carrier into both hands. The medication bag slid against my wrist. Behind us, the veterinarian’s door closed with a small click, and I stood listening to it as though another instruction might come through the wood—something overlooked, something that would change what I was carrying home.

Pip scratched once at his towel.

“All right,” I said. “We’re going.”

In the waiting room, I paid with the card I usually reserved for emergencies. The receptionist tucked the receipt into the medication bag without asking whether I wanted it. I was grateful for that small omission. Outside, the bell trembled above the door, and the harbor air struck my face, cold enough to make my eyes water without explanation.

I took the sheltered side of the road, away from the wind coming between the warehouses. Fishing boats rested low in the harbor. Someone had left a yellow bucket overturned beside the railings, and water dripped steadily from its rim. Everything seemed offensively ordinary until I realized how badly I needed it to be ordinary: the bakery shutting its door, rope creaking against a bollard, somebody sweeping sand from a shop entrance.

At the bait shop, my steps slowed.

I could see the narrow gap where I had first found Pip, tucked behind a stack of empty crates. In memory, I was crouching there again, younger by only a little time and impossibly certain that getting him indoors would solve everything. My phone torch lit two enormous ears. When I reached toward him, he hissed with such determination that I laughed.

“Fair enough,” I had told him. “Stranger danger.”

I had gone home for a towel and returned afraid he would be gone. Instead, he had emerged from behind the crates and attacked the towel’s corner, seemingly forgetting for a moment to fear me. Carrying him upstairs afterward, I had kept saying, “You can stay,” although he had no understanding of tenancy and I had barely learned how to manage my own.

Now I bent slightly over the carrier.

“You can still stay,” I whispered.

Pip blinked through the mesh. I straightened before anyone could ask why I was crying outside a closed bait shop and carried him the rest of the way home.

The stairs demanded care. I held the carrier level against my chest, climbed slowly, and stopped on the landing when my arms began to tremble. Inside the apartment, I set him down before taking off my coat. The room smelled faintly of washing powder and the food I had left covered in the kitchen.

I opened the carrier. Pip put his front paws onto the floor, then hesitated as his back legs followed. One paw slipped on the bare board.

My hand moved beneath his belly before I had time to think.

“Just a second.”

I helped him onto the rug and fetched the matting offcut from beside the wall. The shopkeeper’s gift had seemed generous before; now, kneeling with it across my lap, I felt grateful enough to be embarrassed. I trimmed a loose edge, brushed away the scraps, and laid it between the rug and Pip’s bed. Then I moved his water closer and brought the low-sided litter tray within reach, leaving space between each place.

Pip watched this rearrangement with his ears angled forward.

“Terrible service,” I told him. “Furniture moving while the guest is resting.”

He stepped onto the matting. His claws caught securely, and he crossed it in several slow, uneven steps. I kept my hands nearby but let him finish. At the bed, he sniffed the blanket and climbed in.

I sat back on my heels. It was only a short strip of floor. He still had the illness. Yet he had crossed without slipping, and for a moment I could look at what I had done without immediately seeing everything I could not do.

After offering food, I checked the written instructions and put the medicines where I could reach them without leaving him for long. I saved the clinic’s emergency number in my phone, then copied it onto paper because batteries died and frightened people forgot passwords. Beside the notebook, I left a pen uncapped.

*Home after the clinic,* I wrote. *Ate a little. Crossed the new matting. Resting now.*

Below that, after a pause:

*I keep wanting care to mean getting him well. Tonight it means making the floor easier.*

A thin patch of sunlight reached the bed. Pip lifted his head when my sleeve cast a moving shadow across it. I held still, then moved my wrist a fraction. His paw came up and landed squarely on the shadow.

“Caught it.”

He kept his paw there. I waited until he withdrew it before moving again.

Soon he lowered his chin onto the blanket. I watched his breathing settle, counted as the veterinarian had shown me, and wrote the observation down. Then I put the notebook aside. There would be more things to record, but I wanted him to have some time with my hand empty.

I rested my fingers beside his forepaws.

“Good night, little trouble,” I whispered, though the window was still pale.

The familiar farewell caught in my throat. I bent and kissed the fur between his ears, then stayed on the floor while the sunlight slowly left his bed.


When the room grew dark, I reached up and switched on the little lamp beside the sofa. Pip opened one eye at the click, then closed it again. Beyond the window, the harbor lights made broken yellow paths across the water. I could hear someone fastening a shutter downstairs, followed by footsteps retreating along the empty street.

I had not eaten. Getting up felt like desertion, which was absurd and did not make it easier. I warmed yesterday’s soup and brought it back in a mug. Sitting beside Pip’s bed, I drank with one hand and let him lean against the other. Once, his whiskers stirred toward the steam.

“Absolutely not,” I said. “You have your own dinner.”

His ears turned toward me. I smiled before I remembered I was frightened.

There were more moments like that over the days that followed. Pip licking a smear of food from his nose. Pip objecting when I washed his blanket and substituted a towel. Pip watching a gull on the opposite chimney with an intensity his weakened body could no longer translate into stalking. I brought his bed nearer the window without putting it in the draft, and sat beside him while the gull rearranged its feathers.

*Later,* I wrote in the diary. *He watched the chimney for ages. I opened my coursework beside him and managed half a page. He fell asleep with his paw on the corner.*

I left space beneath the entry, then added: *I am allowed to remember that this was a good afternoon.*

One evening, while searching my phone for the clinic’s number, I touched an old video by mistake. Pip filled the screen, smaller and rounder, pursuing a paper ball beneath the kitchen chair. I heard my own laugh.

I remembered filming it: my knees cold against the boards, the kettle boiling itself hoarse behind me. He had pounced too enthusiastically and landed inside my slipper. For several seconds he stayed there, astonished, while I laughed so hard the picture shook. Afterward, I had carried him against my chest to turn off the kettle. He had bitten a button on my cardigan as though this were his contribution to making tea.

On the bed beside me, the present Pip lifted his head at the recorded sound of my voice.

“Still you,” I whispered, setting the phone aside.

Later, he could not settle. I checked what the veterinarian had written, counted his breaths, and called rather than waiting for morning. We spoke again after the prescribed measures failed to give him lasting relief. I described his efforts to change position, the untouched food, the way he kept raising his head.

“Bring him in,” the veterinarian said gently. “We’ll help him.”

I lined the carrier with his familiar blanket. My fingers fumbled at the door catch, and I had to stop and breathe before lifting him. He weighed so little that I wanted to argue with my own hands.

I carried him down the apartment stairs, pausing at each landing to keep him level. Outside, the town was quiet beneath a low, pale sky. We passed the hardware shop, its window crowded with buckets and coils of rope. I thought of the matting upstairs, the little path that had helped him reach his bed. I was glad I had asked for it.

At the clinic, the veterinarian examined him, then sat with us. They explained what could still be tried and what they believed it would mean for him. I asked my questions twice. They answered twice.

“Can you make him comfortable?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“And if we go home?”

Their answer was careful, but clear. I looked down at Pip, his chin resting in the hollow of my hand.

“I don’t want him to keep struggling,” I said. Agreeing felt unbearable. So did asking him to endure more because I could not bear goodbye.

They brought a soft towel. I put his blanket over it and stayed beside him while the first medicine let his body relax. For the first time that night, his head rested without lifting again.

I told him about the slipper. About the gull. About the abandoned kitten who had frightened me with one magnificent hiss behind the bait shop.

“You were very fierce,” I said, and my voice broke. “I’m so glad I went back for you.”

When the veterinarian asked whether I was ready, I kissed the place between his ears.

“Good night, little trouble. You’re home with me.”

I kept my hand around his paw through the last injection, and afterward, until the veterinarian quietly told me his heart had stopped. There was no answer I needed to give. I stayed.

Back upstairs, I set the empty carrier beside the door. The matting still led to his bed. I could not put either away.

I opened the diary beneath the lamp.

*Pip died with my hand around his paw. He was comfortable. I miss him already.*

For a while, that was all I could write. Then I turned back through the pages—food, medicines, breath counts—until I found the photograph of him upside down in the sun.

I placed it beside the last entry, leaving both in view.

prompt: Write a story about someone who faces unexplained weight gain and runs into trainers and doctors who don’t take them seriously. Explore themes of resilience, self-advocacy, and the journey from patient to healer. Set it in today’s fitness and medical world, include a breakthrough moment with a compassionate specialist, and show how this experience inspires them to become a supportive trainer.

chapters.text:
The chair in the endocrinology waiting room had arms that pressed against my hips. I sat forward, keeping my coat on my lap, and tried not to take that personally. Across from me, a screen advertised a wellness app: a woman running uphill beneath the words TAKE CONTROL. My phone vibrated with a notification from my own fitness app. I turned it facedown before it could congratulate me or tell me what I had failed to do.

In my tote bag was a folder thick enough to feel embarrassing. Appointment summaries, lab results, a list of medications, and the timeline I had rewritten so it would fit on one page. Thirty-one pounds gained without an explanation. Walks that had grown shorter despite my efforts to make them longer. Cold hands. Constipation. Exhaustion that sleep barely touched. I had put the symptoms before the weight this time.

At the gym, my trainer had scrolled through my food log while I stood beside the cable machine, holding a towel.

“People forget the little things,” he’d said. “Oil. Coffee creamer. A handful of nuts.”

“I measure the oil.”

He had smiled with a patience that made me feel worse than irritation would have. “Then we need to talk about honesty.”

I still heard that word while cooking, while buying groceries, while waking tired after nine hours in bed. Honesty had become something I apparently owed everybody except myself.

The first doctor had suggested an exercise program. The second had suggested that my exercise program wasn’t rigorous enough. Neither had asked why climbing the stairs to my apartment now left my thighs trembling. At the last appointment, I had started crying and watched the conversation turn toward stress. Stress was real; I had plenty. But I had arrived with more than one symptom, and I wanted more than one possibility considered.

When the nurse called my name, I stood too quickly and caught the chair arm.

“Take your time,” she said.

I followed her down a hallway smelling faintly of disinfectant and coffee. At the scale, I asked, “Could you not say the number out loud?”

“Of course.”

Such a small accommodation. I nearly thanked her twice.

Dr. Rao entered the exam room carrying a tablet, but she set it on the desk before sitting down. I noticed that immediately. Most people who had questioned me about my body had kept their eyes on a screen.

“What would make this appointment useful to you?” she asked.

I had prepared for *What brings you in?* I had not prepared for useful.

“I want to know why I’m gaining weight,” I said. “But I also want to be able to get through a workday without feeling like somebody unplugged me.”

She waited.

“And I need you to believe I’m trying.”

My voice cracked on the last word. I looked at the folder instead of her face.

“Trying isn’t something you have to prove before you deserve an evaluation,” she said. “May I see what you brought?”

I handed it over. While she read, I watched her turn each page rather than merely lift the corners. She asked when the fatigue had begun, whether my periods had changed, whether I took supplements, whether I snored. Some questions surprised me. None sounded like a trap. When I couldn’t remember something, she gave me time to check my notes.

She stopped at an older lab report.

“Were these results discussed with you?”

“The message said there was nothing urgent.”

She moved her chair so we could look together. One thyroid result sat just beyond the laboratory’s reference range. I had seen the tiny flag beside it before, but the reassuring portal message had made me set it aside.

“This alone doesn’t establish a diagnosis,” she said. “A mild elevation can be temporary. But with the symptoms you’re describing, it deserves follow-up. I’d like to repeat your thyroid tests, including free T4, and check a few other possible contributors to the fatigue.”

“So there’s something to investigate?”

“Yes,” she said. “There is.”

I pressed my thumb into the folder’s bent corner. I wasn’t relieved exactly. I wanted normal results and an answer, two wishes that might not fit together. Still, for the first time, I could picture a next appointment that wasn’t simply another opportunity to disappoint someone.

“What should I do about training?”

“Tell me what happens when you exercise.”

I described the shaking, the prolonged soreness, the trainer urging me through another circuit.

“For now, don’t push through dizziness or unusual weakness,” she said. “We can work out an activity plan while we investigate. Movement doesn’t need to be punishment.”

I thought of the woman at my gym who always apologized before taking the lighter dumbbells. I had nodded along instead of telling her there was nothing to apologize for. Sitting there, I wondered what it would take to become the sort of trainer who asked questions before giving instructions.

Before I left, I asked when to expect the results and who would contact me. Dr. Rao wrote down the plan, then handed me the page to check.

I read it carefully.

“Can we add the leg weakness?” I asked.

She uncapped her pen. “Absolutely.”


I read the additions twice before giving the page back. Dr. Rao had written *leg weakness with exertion* beneath the list of blood tests, then added a note about contacting the clinic if the weakness worsened or came with fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing. The warning did not frighten me as much as the absence of one would have. It made the appointment feel like a real plan instead of a polite dismissal.

“Will the activity plan come from you?” I asked.

“Partly,” she said. “Once we know more, I may refer you to physical therapy or a dietitian who understands medical weight changes. For now, I’d like you to track what you can tolerate, not what an app says you should tolerate.”

I opened my phone and showed her the exercise summary from the previous week. The colored rings were mostly gray. A red banner announced that I had missed my movement goal three days in a row.

“This makes me feel as if I’m failing,” I admitted.

“Then it isn’t useful data in its current form.” She pointed to the notes section. “Record the activity, how long you did it, and what happened afterward. If ten minutes of walking leaves you shaky for hours, that matters. If stretching helps, that matters too. The purpose is to observe your body, not grade it.”

I typed the words into my notes while she spoke. *Observe, don’t grade.* They looked almost rebellious beside the app’s demand to close my rings.

A knock sounded, and the nurse appeared with a small paper cup and a label sheet. “The lab can see you now,” she said. “Would you like someone to walk with you, or are you comfortable going down the hall?”

“I’m comfortable walking,” I said, then glanced at Dr. Rao. “As long as I can sit if I need to.”

“Absolutely,” the nurse replied. “There are chairs outside the draw room.”

She did not say it as if I were making a dramatic request. She said it as if chairs existed for exactly that reason. I tucked the plan into my folder, stood carefully, and waited for the brief gray shimmer at the edge of my vision to pass. It did. Dr. Rao watched without rushing me.

“Tell the lab technician about the weakness,” she said. “And don’t drive if you feel unsafe afterward.”

“I will.”

The nurse led me out of the endocrinology exam room and into the hallway, making the transition as ordinary as possible. The clinic’s doors opened and closed around us; phones rang at the front desk; someone’s printer clicked through a stack of insurance forms. At the lab window, I handed over my paperwork and confirmed that the results would appear in the patient portal. The staff member explained that some tests might return before others and that the clinic would contact me when Dr. Rao had reviewed them.

I almost laughed at the phrase *when Dr. Rao had reviewed them*. My previous results had arrived as an automated notification with a green checkmark and no explanation. This time I wrote down the clinic number and asked what to do if I had questions before the follow-up.

“You can send a portal message,” the nurse said. “Use the symptom details rather than just saying you feel worse. It helps the team triage it.”

That advice landed harder than she could have known. For months, I had edited myself into acceptable sentences: *I’m tired. I’m gaining weight. I’m trying.* Now I opened a blank note and began listing the details—stairs, trembling thighs, soreness that lasted two days, the point at which walking stopped feeling restorative and started feeling dangerous.

When the phlebotomist called me in, I sat in the chair with my folder on my lap. She checked my name and birth date, explained each tube, and asked which arm I preferred. I chose the left. As the needle went in, I watched the dark blood fill the first vial and thought about how much effort had gone into proving I was not secretly careless. Food logs. Weigh-ins. Workout screenshots. Apologies to trainers. Silence in examination rooms.

I knew the blood tests would not tell the whole story. Even the thyroid result, if it came back abnormal again, might be one piece rather than the answer. But investigation was different from accusation. I could feel that difference in my shoulders, which had lowered for the first time all morning.

Afterward, I remained seated until the nurse said I looked steady. She offered crackers and water. I accepted both, then sent the portal message while the instructions were fresh: *I completed the labs today. I’m also tracking the leg weakness as discussed. Please let me know if you need anything else before follow-up.*

Outside the clinic, I stopped beneath the awning instead of heading straight to the parking lot. My phone buzzed with a message from the gym reminding me about the evening circuit. I opened it, stared at the list of timed exercises, and canceled.

For once, canceling was not surrender. It was an action based on information I had gathered. I put the phone away and walked slowly toward my car, carrying Dr. Rao’s plan in my folder and a different kind of plan beginning in my head: if I ever trained people, I would ask what happened after the workout, not just whether they completed it.


At my car, I put the folder on the passenger seat and waited before turning the key. My legs felt tired, but the trembling had settled. I drank the rest of the water the nurse had given me, checked that I felt clearheaded, and drove home without stopping at the gym to explain myself.

That omission felt enormous. Usually I would have gone inside, shown my face, offered some proof that canceling had cost me something. Instead, I parked outside my apartment and carried only my tote upstairs, leaving a bag of laundry in the trunk. Halfway up, I paused on the landing. Someone had propped a delivery box against the railing; I stood beside it until my thighs stopped quivering. Upstairs, I recorded the stairs, the pause, and how long recovery seemed to take. I did not add a verdict.

My phone rang while I was taking bread out of the freezer. The gym’s number filled the screen. For a moment I considered letting it go to voicemail, but I wanted to know whether canceling had used the last session in my package.

“Hey,” my trainer said when I answered. Music thudded behind his voice. “Saw you dropped tonight. Everything okay?”

“I had a medical appointment. I’m changing my activity while we investigate the weakness.”

“Sure. We can modify. Getting here is the main thing.”

I pressed the frozen slices apart with my thumb. That had once sounded encouraging. Now I heard how little room it left for the possibility that getting there wasn’t the right goal.

“I’m not coming tonight.”

A brief silence followed.

“You’ve missed a few lately. Consistency matters more than intensity. We don’t want to lose momentum.”

I set the bread down. “I understand consistency. I’m having symptoms that need evaluating.”

“Have you been eating enough protein?”

The question might have been reasonable somewhere else, from someone else. Coming after months of doubt about what I ate, it made my face grow hot.

“My doctor and I have a plan,” I said. “I need to pause our sessions. Can the unused ones stay on my account?”

“I can ask the manager. But if you wait until you feel motivated—”

“This isn’t about motivation.”

My voice came out louder than I intended. I looked toward the open kitchen window, embarrassed even with nobody there.

“I’m not asking you to diagnose anything,” I continued. “I’m asking you to respect that I’m not doing circuits while ordinary stairs leave my legs shaking.”

The music on his end dipped, then swelled again.

“Okay,” he said. “Send the pause request through the app. I’ll flag it.”

I thanked him automatically. After we hung up, I disliked the thank-you, then disliked myself for policing even that. A conversation did not have to be perfectly brave to count. I had said what I needed and stayed with it.

In the app, the pause form required a reason. The choices were travel, injury, financial, and other. I chose other and wrote, *Medical evaluation in progress. Requesting a temporary pause in training.* I nearly attached the lab order before realizing the gym did not need my medical record. I submitted the request without it, saved the confirmation, and switched off workout reminders.

The kitchen became strangely quiet. I toasted the bread, made eggs, and ate sitting down instead of standing over the counter. My folder lay beside the plate. Under it was an older appointment summary with the same recommendation I remembered: increase physical activity. There was no mention of the stairs. I turned the page over rather than read it again.

After lunch, I opened my laptop and searched for personal-training qualifications. The results came crowded with promises: transform lives, build your brand, become your own boss. One advertisement showed a trainer shouting beside a sweating client. I scrolled past it and opened a course outline.

Anatomy. Exercise programming. Screening. Scope of practice. CPR and first aid.

Until then, becoming a trainer had been a thought I visited when I wanted to imagine a kinder gym. The list made it work: study, money, assessments, skills I did not yet have. I checked the price and winced. Then I opened a blank document titled *Questions before enrolling*.

Could I study part-time? How did practical assessments work? What training addressed chronic illness and referral to qualified clinicians? I added another question: how did a trainer learn to distinguish ordinary effort from a reason to stop, without pretending to be a doctor?

I pictured the woman who apologized for choosing lighter dumbbells. I had no idea what she needed beyond permission to choose them. That was the point. I would have to ask.

A portal notification interrupted me. My stomach tightened before I opened it. It was an acknowledgment from the clinic: my message had been received; results were still pending review.

No answer yet. I put the phone beside Dr. Rao’s instructions and added the afternoon’s fatigue to my log. Then I returned to the course website, found the admissions contact form, and typed my first question.


The admissions form remained open while the apartment darkened around me. I read my question again: *How does your program accommodate students who need to study part-time or who have a medical condition affecting exercise tolerance?* My finger hovered over the Submit button. The course website had made everything sound simple—watch the modules, pass the assessment, start helping people—but I no longer trusted simple promises.

I added a second question before sending it: *What is the boundary between a trainer’s responsibility and a clinician’s?* Then I attached no medical documents, described no diagnosis, and wrote only that I was currently undergoing evaluation for fatigue and exertional weakness. The wording felt careful rather than secretive. I was allowed to ask about a course without turning my body into an application essay.

I pressed Submit. A confirmation appeared immediately, promising that someone would respond through email. I saved a screenshot beside the clinic portal acknowledgment. Two messages, both saying essentially the same thing: received, not yet reviewed. The parallel made my chest tighten. I wanted an answer from Dr. Rao, an answer from the school, an answer from my own body. Instead, I had to tolerate the space between asking and knowing.

The next morning, I woke with the heavy sensation that had become familiar but never normal. My calves felt packed with wet sand. When I sat up, I waited for the room to steady before standing. I walked to the bathroom, brushed my teeth, and recorded the effort afterward: *short walk inside apartment; legs weak but no dizziness; rested four minutes.* The old version of me would have called that an embarrassing amount of information. Dr. Rao had called it useful data, and I was trying to believe her.

By breakfast, the gym app had sent another automated reminder. *Your body is capable of more than you think.* I stared at the sentence until its encouragement turned accusatory. Then I opened the pause request and checked its status. *Under review.* No promise about preserving the unused sessions appeared, but the request existed outside my head now. I forwarded the confirmation to myself and created a folder titled *Health and Training Records*. Into it went the clinic message, my symptom log, the gym request, and the course questions.

The organization did not cure anything. My weight had not dropped. My legs did not suddenly become reliable. But arranging the documents gave the uncertainty edges. I could see what I had reported, what had been ordered, and what remained unanswered. I was not waiting passively for a verdict; I was preparing to participate in the next conversation.

When my phone rang, I expected the gym. It was the clinic’s number. I answered carefully.

“Hello?”

“This is the clinic calling to confirm that Dr. Rao has received your message,” a staff member said. “Your laboratory results are still pending review. Some values have posted, but she wants to look at the complete panel before commenting.”

“Thank you for letting me know.” I glanced at the folder on the table. “Should I continue tracking the weakness?”

“Yes. Please include what activity you did and how you felt afterward. If you develop severe weakness, fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing, seek urgent care.”

“I understand.”

The call ended without a diagnosis, but not without meaning. The clinic had not lost my message in a digital queue. Dr. Rao was waiting for the complete information, just as I was. I wrote down the call, including the phrase *complete panel*, and resisted the temptation to open the portal every few minutes.

Instead, I followed the activity instructions she had given me. I filled a glass of water, moved through the gentle stretches, and stopped after the second one when my thighs began to quiver. I sat on the edge of the couch and watched the timer. The shaking eased after several minutes, but the tiredness stayed. I recorded both facts. Stopping had not been failure. Continuing would not have proved courage.

An email arrived from the training program while I was writing. The subject line read, *Your admissions question has been received.* It offered no answer yet, only a reference number and a note that an advisor would respond. I laughed once, softly, at the absurdity of collecting confirmations instead of solutions. Then I added the email to the folder.

My local plan changed as I typed beneath it: *Do not enroll until I understand the schedule, practical requirements, accessibility, and scope-of-practice education.* That was not abandoning the idea of becoming a trainer. It was the first responsible step toward it.

I opened a new page and wrote the questions I would ask if an advisor called. Would students practice screening without treating it as diagnosis? Were they taught how to refer someone back to a doctor? Could a client modify an exercise without being labeled uncommitted? What did the program say about weight-neutral coaching, fatigue, and conditions that were not visible?

My hand paused over the last question. I remembered the trainers who had told me to push through, the doctors who had glanced at my weight and assumed the explanation was obvious, and the moments when I had started believing them. If I became a trainer, I could not promise every client an answer. I could promise to listen before prescribing effort.

The portal still showed *results pending review*. I left it unopened after that. I put on loose clothes, carried my water to the chair by the window, and continued the symptom log while the afternoon passed. My body remained unexplained, but my next action was clear: wait for Dr. Rao’s review, keep gathering accurate information, and learn how to make room for someone else’s truth before asking them to move.


The apartment stayed quiet after the clinic call, but quiet no longer felt restful. It gave every notification room to become important. I placed my phone face down on the table and opened the symptom log instead. The last entry read: *Gentle stretches, stopped when thighs quivered; shaking eased after several minutes; fatigue continued.* Beneath it, I added the time I had spent sitting afterward and the heaviness that remained in my legs. I was learning to record the whole effect, not just the moment that made me stop.

The scale waited beside the bathroom cabinet. I had moved it there weeks ago after avoiding it for several days, hoping proximity would make the number less frightening. It had not. My weight had climbed despite the meals I logged, the sessions I attended, and the effort I kept making when effort was supposed to explain everything. I stepped on, wrote down the result without changing the entry, and stepped off. The number was information, not a confession. I repeated the sentence silently until it sounded less like something borrowed from a wellness post.

My phone buzzed before I had returned to the couch. The gym had replied to my pause request. *We can place your membership sessions on temporary hold. Please provide a medical note and an estimated return date.* I read it twice. The message was more polite than my trainer’s comments had been, but the demand still made my shoulders tighten. I did not have a diagnosis to submit. I did not know when I would return. The entire reason for pausing was that I could not responsibly promise either.

I opened the reply box and typed, *I am currently undergoing medical evaluation, and my clinician has not provided a return date. I can provide confirmation that an evaluation is in progress, but I am not authorizing release of laboratory results or other medical records.* My finger hovered over Send. The old fear rose quickly: they will think I am difficult; they will say I am making excuses; they will cancel the sessions because I cannot prove I deserve rest.

I sent it anyway. Then I added a second sentence asking them to identify the policy requiring a return date and to confirm whether unused sessions would remain available while the request was reviewed. The wording was plain, almost formal. It did not accuse anyone. It also did not apologize. I saved a copy in the records folder and wrote, *Pause request now includes boundary about private medical information.* That was a small advance, but it was an advance I could point to.

The reply came while I was still staring at the folder. The manager had not approved the request yet, but the sessions would not be erased during review. I let out a breath I had not noticed holding. Nothing about my body had changed. The laboratory panel was still pending. Dr. Rao still had to review it. Yet the gym could no longer turn an unanswered request into a lost package while I waited.

I made tea and carried it to the desk, moving slowly because my legs felt less steady than they had before the stretches. Halfway there, a tremor began in my right thigh. I set the mug down, braced one hand against the desk, and sat before the shaking intensified. I started the timer on my phone. The weakness was not dramatic enough for a movie, only a quivering muscle and the stubborn need to stop doing something ordinary. After five minutes, I stood carefully and finished the short walk to the chair by the window. I recorded the activity, the tremor, and the recovery time.

I reopened the admissions website on my laptop. Beneath the cheerful photograph of a trainer demonstrating a squat, I reread the course description: practical coaching, client assessment, exercise modification, professional conduct. I copied the contact information into my notes and drafted a message instead of enrolling. *Before I apply, I need to understand how students are taught to respond when a client reports unusual fatigue or weakness. What is the process for referring a client back to a clinician? How are modifications handled when attendance or performance is affected by health? Are instructors prepared to teach weight-neutral coaching rather than treating weight loss as the automatic outcome?*

I read the draft aloud. The questions sounded demanding, but not unreasonable. I added one more: *Can practical assessments be adapted or rescheduled when a student is following a clinician’s activity restrictions?* Then I saved the message without sending it. My plan was no longer “sign up and hope.” It was “ask, verify, and decide.” That difference steadied me.

A second clinic notification appeared, and my stomach clenched. I opened it carefully. It only confirmed that the laboratory panel remained in process and that Dr. Rao would review the complete results when available. No diagnosis, no explanation, no sudden answer to the weight gain or the fatigue. I closed the portal and placed the phone beside the log. Waiting was still part of the plan, not evidence that I had been forgotten.

Before turning off the laptop, I wrote a local replan beneath the unanswered questions: *Pause training. Continue gentle activity only as instructed. Track exertional weakness and post-activity effects. Await laboratory results and Dr. Rao’s review. Do not enroll until the program explains its medical boundaries.* The list did not make me well, but it kept other people’s assumptions from becoming my instructions. I leaned back, tired from the short walk and the decisions, and let the apartment remain quiet without mistaking quiet for surrender.


The next morning, I opened the saved message to the training program before checking the clinic portal. My questions filled most of the screen. I removed the sentence explaining how hard I had tried to keep exercising. It had nothing to do with whether a school taught safe practice. Then I pressed Send, put the laptop aside, and walked from the chair by the window to the kitchen table, carrying only my phone. The notebook could wait until I had eaten.

Bread caught in the toaster. I eased it loose with the appliance unplugged, annoyed by how even breakfast had acquired extra steps. On the counter, my old shaker bottle stood behind the kettle. My trainer had once tapped its lid and asked whether I was counting “the little extras” when I mentioned the weight gain. At the time, I had emptied my bag to show him the label on the protein powder. Remembering that now, I left the bottle where it was and spread butter on my toast.

The clinic number appeared while I was pulling out the kitchen chair.

“Is this a good time?” Dr. Rao asked. “I’m calling from my office. Your complete panel isn’t available yet, but I’ve read your update about the weakness.”

I sat down. “It eased after I rested. I wasn’t sure whether that made it less important.”

“It matters that it improved. It also matters that it happened.”

My hand tightened around the phone. She asked whether I was weak now, whether I could walk as usual, whether there had been numbness, pain, or any other change. I answered slowly, resisting the urge to round everything down. The right-thigh shaking had stopped. The heaviness remained. I could move around the apartment, but ordinary tasks took more effort than they used to.

“Thank you for being specific,” she said. “Please don’t repeat an activity to prove the symptom happens. Your description is enough for us to act on.”

I looked at the stretch of floor between the table and the counter. Some part of me had been considering exactly that: another walk, timed more accurately, perhaps evidence no one could dismiss.

“So I don’t need a video?”

“Not if obtaining one means provoking weakness or risking a fall. If the weakness returns or worsens, contact us promptly so we can decide where you need to be assessed. Sudden or persistent one-sided weakness needs emergency assessment, especially with speech or facial changes. Don’t wait for a portal reply.”

I repeated the instructions back. She corrected one detail, and I wrote them on the clean edge of an envelope. Then I asked the question I had avoided at every appointment before hers.

“If the thyroid results don’t explain this, what happens?”

“Then we keep evaluating,” she said. “We review what they do tell us, examine you again as needed, and consider other causes. A test that doesn’t explain a symptom doesn’t make the symptom disappear.”

The refrigerator hummed behind me. I watched a drop of water slide down the kettle and tried to answer without crying.

“The other doctor said I probably wasn’t aware of how much I was eating.”

“Food and activity can be relevant to health,” she said. “But they aren’t substitutes for investigating a change in weight accompanied by fatigue and weakness. You deserve that investigation.”

Nothing in the kitchen changed. My toast had gone cold. My legs still felt heavy beneath the table. Yet I no longer had to spend the whole conversation establishing that there was a problem. We could talk about what to do next.
