The nurse heard only my spoken part. “What did you say?”

“I was telling myself not to turn this into a test.”

“That’s a good rule.” She glanced toward the chair by the window. “You’ve been in bed since I helped you back. Would you like to change position, or would you rather rest?”

The chair’s presence became an invitation rather than a challenge. I checked the shoulder, the room, and the distance between the mattress and the floor. “I think I can move to the chair if we do it slowly. But I want to stop if the shoulder tires again.”

“Then we’ll make that the plan. You call the stop. I’ll handle the lines.”

She raised the bed and moved the chair closer before asking me to do anything. The wheels clicked as she locked them. That small sound made the transition real: I was no longer merely imagining movement from the hospital bed to the chair. The space between them had been cleared, the tubing gathered, and assistance stood ready.

“Feet first,” she said. “No rushing.”

I brought my legs toward the edge, pausing when the pull reached my shoulder. The heart urged me to say so, and I did.

“Pause. It’s heavier.”

The nurse stopped immediately and waited. I breathed in through my nose and let the lungs set the pace. No voice counted. I counted nothing. After several breaths, the heaviness eased enough for me to continue.

My feet touched the floor. The hospital tile looked farther away than it had earlier, though I knew the distance had not changed. The nurse positioned herself beside me and supported my arm without lifting it beyond what felt safe.

“Ready to stand?”

“Not yet.”

The precise voice offered a sequence. I accepted only the first instruction: lean forward. I shifted my weight, pressed through my feet, and rose with the nurse’s help. My knees shook, but they held. The monitor continued its measured beeping, and the IV pole rolled beside us.

“Shoulder?” she asked.

“Tired, not worse.”

“Then one step.”

I moved toward the chair. The first step felt deliberate; the second felt possible. When the backs of my legs touched the seat, I stopped. The nurse guided me down, and I settled into the cushion with a breath that trembled on the way out.

The lungs made room. The heart did not demand more. Even the stomach stayed quiet.

I looked back at the bed, then at the space I had crossed. It was only a few feet of hospital floor, but I had not crossed it by force or impatience. I had noticed the warning, called for help, and changed positions before the pain made the decision for me.

“Water?” I asked.

“I’ll bring it within reach,” the nurse said. “And you remember the rule.”

“I call before I move again.”

“Exactly.”

She secured the lines and placed the call button on the chair’s armrest. I curled my fingers around it without pressing. The chair held me differently than the bed did, and the room opened around that difference. I was still injured, still dependent on careful assistance, but I had advanced one task without letting any single part of me take control.


The chair held me differently than the bed did, and the room opened around that difference. I kept my fingers around the call button without pressing it. The nurse had gone to bring water, but I did not let the promise of it turn into a reason to reach for anything. The cup on the over-bed table was close enough to tempt me. Close enough, I reminded myself, was not the same as safe.

“Thirst is increasing,” said the precise voice.

“Not an emergency,” I answered silently.

“Water would support recovery.”

“Then we wait for assistance.”

The heart gave a slow, even beat. “Good. Say what changes. Don’t hide it.”

I checked the shoulder. The heaviness remained, but it had not worsened. My back ached from holding myself upright, and my legs felt unsteady beneath the chair, though I was not standing. I reported each sensation aloud, partly for the nurse when she returned and partly so the voices would have facts instead of guesses.

“Shoulder tired. Back sore. No dizziness. Breathing steady.”

The lungs widened beneath my ribs. They did not need to argue for space; I gave it to them by relaxing my neck and letting the breath arrive without forcing it. The room smelled faintly of disinfectant and broth. Somewhere beyond the door, a cart rattled over a seam in the floor, then faded.

The call button crackled before I touched it. “I’m back,” the nurse said from the doorway.

She carried a plastic cup with a lid and straw, but she did not hand it over immediately. First she checked the IV line, the monitor, and the position of my injured arm. Then she brought the table closer and set the cup where I could see it without leaning.

“How are you feeling in the chair?”

“Stable, but my back is getting sore. The shoulder is still tired.”

“Any increase?”

“No.”

“Good. We’ll work with stable.” She loosened the blanket over my knees. “Would you like to stay here a little longer, or return to the bed?”

I looked toward the bed. It seemed both inviting and farther away than before. Returning would be a movement, not a retreat, but I did not want to make the decision simply because the chair had become uncomfortable.

“The goal was to change position,” I said. “I’ve done that. I think I can stay if we adjust the chair.”

“We can move it closer to the table and angle it so your back is supported. I’ll do the pushing. You won’t need to stand.”

The precise voice began producing instructions anyway. “Place feet, release brake, maintain—”

“No counting,” I told it. “And no commands unless I ask.”

The nurse glanced at me, perhaps hearing only the last sentence. “You’re in charge of the limits.”

That steadied me. She checked the call button again and asked me to tell her before she touched the frame. I nodded. She released the brake, keeping one hand on the chair back and the other near my shoulder without pulling. The wheels rolled a few inches across the hospital floor. The movement was small, but I felt the shift through my spine and the faint tug where the tubing followed.

“Heaviness?” she asked.

“Still the same.”

She stopped immediately, though the chair had not yet reached the table. I took a breath, then another. The lungs set a calm rhythm. The heart encouraged honesty rather than speed.

“Can we continue?”

“Yes,” she said. “Only if you say so.”

I gave permission. The nurse rolled the chair the remaining distance and turned it slightly toward the window. The transition was complete: I had moved from the first position beside the bed to a supported place nearer the table, without standing or reaching. The window showed a pale slice of sky between neighboring hospital walls. I could not see beyond that, but the light changed across the floor as the chair settled.

The nurse placed the straw near my mouth. I took a small sip, then paused. The water was cool, and my throat accepted it without difficulty. I waited for nausea, dizziness, or a sharper pull in the shoulder. None came.

“Another?” she asked.

“After a breath.”

She waited. That patience mattered more than the water. The stomach stirred hopefully, asking whether food might follow. I remembered the broth and crackers, the way half a meal had been enough because enough was allowed to be enough.

“Could I have more broth later?” I asked. “If the medication and water continue to sit well?”

“I’ll check what’s available and bring another light serving. We’ll keep it small.”

The stomach settled at the promise. The heart remained measured.

I took a second sip, then lowered my chin rather than reaching for the cup. “That’s enough for now.”

The nurse set the cup in its holder. “You made that call yourself.”

“I’m trying to notice the limit before it becomes a problem.”

“That’s the work.”

The precise voice offered a conclusion, but I interrupted it before it could turn the moment into a formula. “The work is shared,” I said.

The nurse adjusted the blanket and checked the shoulder one more time. I could feel the internal voices aligning—not silent, not identical, but no longer pulling me in separate directions. The lungs had room, the heart had a steady task, the stomach had a modest plan, and I had the call button under my hand.

I remained in the chair, angled toward the window, and let the hospital move around me without demanding that I keep pace. I had changed position safely, asked for water, and made room for food without forcing either. The next movement would wait for another call.


The room remained arranged around the chair: the table within reach but not within tempting distance, the call button beneath my fingers, the IV line looped safely along the armrest. I kept my eyes on the cup while I waited for my body to answer the second sip. The water had gone down cleanly. My throat felt less dry, and the stomach had not objected. Still, I refused to turn tolerance into permission for haste.

“Any change?” the heart asked.

“Not yet,” I said silently, then aloud, because the nurse had stayed near the counter while checking the chart. “No nausea. No dizziness. The shoulder is heavy, but not heavier.”

She looked up. “Good reporting. Give it another minute before we decide about the broth.”

The precise voice supplied a list of reasons the minute mattered. I stopped it with a thought before the list grew teeth. “One reason is enough.”

“One reason,” it answered. “We are testing whether the medication and water remain settled.”

“That’s useful.”

The room’s monitor continued its patient rhythm. I listened to it without trying to match my heartbeat to the sound. The lungs drew in a shallow breath, then a fuller one when I lowered my shoulders. The chair supported my back more effectively after the adjustment, but the position still made my injured side aware of every small shift. I did not move to escape the awareness. I let it report.

The nurse came closer and examined my face. “How is the pain now?”

“Still manageable. The shoulder feels tired. The back soreness is better since you angled the chair.”

“Any sharper pain with the water?”

“No.”

“Then I’ll bring a small serving of broth. I’ll also check whether your medication is due. You stay exactly where you are.”

“I will.”

She left through the open doorway. Her footsteps moved only a short distance down the corridor before blending with the hospital sounds: a cart rolling, a distant call bell, someone speaking softly at a station. The open doorway framed a rectangle of brighter light, but I remained inside the recovery room. Nothing about the hallway invited me to follow. The next task was not walking. It was receiving what my body could use without making it prove anything.

The stomach gave a cautious murmur.

“Patience,” I told it.

“I am patient,” it replied. “I am also ready.”

The heart answered with a steady pressure beneath my ribs. “Ready is not the same as empty.”

That was true enough to make me smile. The smile tugged at my shoulder, and I stopped it before it became a grimace. The heart noticed.

“Pain changed?” it asked.

“Only from the movement in my face. It settled.”

I pressed the call button once, not because I needed the nurse immediately, but because I wanted to make sure it remained accessible. The tiny indicator lit under my thumb. The action reassured me more than it should have. Assistance was not an abstract promise. It was a button, a voice, a person who had already stopped a chair when I said the heaviness remained.

The nurse returned carrying a shallow bowl on a tray. Steam rose in a thin veil. She set it on the table and waited before bringing it nearer.

“Medication is being prepared,” she said. “The broth is plain. We’ll start with a few spoonfuls.”

“Can I hold the spoon?”

“If your shoulder stays comfortable. I can assist.”

I considered the distance between my hand and the bowl. It was small, but the arm would have to lift and turn. “You assist,” I said. “I don’t want to spend the shoulder on the reaching.”

“Good choice.”

She placed a folded towel beneath my elbow and guided the spoon. The broth touched my tongue, warm and salty, and my stomach accepted it with a quiet settling. I waited through one breath, then another.

“Any trouble?” she asked.

“No. Another.”

The second spoonful went as smoothly as the first. By the third, the warmth had spread through me without becoming heaviness. I reported that too. The precise voice tried to calculate how many spoonfuls would constitute a serving, and I refused the number.

“We’re not finishing the bowl,” I said.

The nurse nodded. “Small is the plan.”

The heart seemed to ease, not because it had won, but because no part of me had needed to win. I took two more spoonfuls, then lifted my free hand slightly.

“Pause.”

The nurse set the spoon down at once. I waited for the shoulder’s answer. Fatigue remained, but there was no climb in pain, no dizziness, no nausea. The lungs moved easily enough for me to speak.

“That’s enough until the medication is here.”

The nurse covered the bowl and moved it to the table’s edge, still close but no longer in front of me. “We’ll let that settle. When the medication arrives, we’ll decide whether you stay in the chair or return to bed. Either way, you call before moving.”

“I will.”

She checked the IV line and placed the call button squarely beneath my palm again. I looked toward the bed, then back at the chair. The distance between them was unchanged, but the decision no longer felt urgent. I had asked for help, accepted food in a measured amount, and kept the shoulder from becoming the leader of the next step.

For now, the chair held me, the broth waited, and the hospital continued its work around us.


The towel beneath my elbow had begun to feel too thin. I noticed it before the ache changed: a growing awareness of the chair arm, the work of keeping my shoulder still. The covered broth sat at the table’s edge. Five spoonfuls remained five spoonfuls; I had not become nauseated by waiting, and I did not need another taste to prove they had settled.

“Report the shoulder,” the heart said.

“It’s tired.”

“Tell her.”

The nurse had stepped outside to collect the medication. I pressed the call button and left my hand where it was. When a voice answered, I said, “I’d like help getting back into bed. My shoulder is tiring. I haven’t tried to stand.”

“We’ll be right there.”

The precise voice began, “A transfer requires several coordinated—”

“One instruction at a time,” I told it silently. “And hers first.”

For once, the pause that followed felt less like resistance than attention. I looked at the bed without measuring the distance. The blanket lay folded back where I had left it. From the chair, I could see a crease in the pillowcase that had been invisible while my head rested there.

The nurse returned with a small medication cup and checked my wristband against the screen. “You called before it got worse?”

“Yes. No sharper pain. Just more effort holding this position.”

“That’s enough reason to change it.” She set the cup on the counter. “We’ll get you supported in bed first, then give you this while you’re sitting up.”

“Will that interfere with the broth?”

“Not with what you’ve had. Tell me if you’re feeling sick.”

“I’m not.”

The stomach stirred. “There is still broth.”

“And there will still be a stomach after we move,” the heart replied.

I nearly laughed, then spared myself the tug. “Food can wait,” I said. The nurse nodded and moved the table away, taking both the covered bowl and the water out of our path. The small clearance made the journey look possible, but when she asked me to wait while she brought another staff member, I stayed seated.

They returned together. The nurse explained the movement, then asked me to repeat the part I needed to remember. I would keep my injured arm supported, use only the support they indicated, and tell them immediately if I felt dizzy or the pain changed. They arranged the tubing, secured the chair, and brought the bed to a suitable height.

The precise voice offered, “Watch where your feet are.”

“That helps,” I answered silently.

“Breathe out with the effort,” the lungs said.

That helped too. Neither instruction required me to become brave before I could obey it.

At the nurse’s cue, I leaned forward with their assistance. The shift brought a dull pull through my side, and I stopped.

“Pulling,” I said.

Both helpers held still.

“Sharp?” the nurse asked.

“No. Let me settle.”

My heart beat harder. I heard the monitor quicken and wanted to apologize for it, as though I had made extra work by having a body. Instead, I let a breath leave me.

“Still here,” the heart said.

“Room for the next breath,” said the lungs.

The pulling eased when the nurse adjusted the support at my arm. I told her so. Only then did we continue.

Standing was brief and untidy. My knees trembled; the floor seemed farther down than it should have been. With a person steadying me on either side, I took the small turning steps toward the bed. The nurse managed the line as we moved. I felt the mattress against the backs of my legs before she told me to sit.

I lowered myself with their help. The mattress received my weight, and I stayed on its edge while they checked how I felt.

“No dizziness,” I said. “Shoulder’s sore, but not sharp.”

They helped lift my legs and ease me back against the raised head of the bed. A pillow went beneath the injured arm. The relief was immediate enough that I closed my eyes, then opened them when the nurse asked another question.

“Better supported?”

“Yes. Much.”

She checked the line again. The other staff member left after making sure I was settled, and the nurse brought the medication cup from the counter. She explained what she was giving me, then helped with the water. I swallowed, paused, and accepted another small sip to clear the taste.

The precise voice started to count the seconds.

“No,” I said inwardly. “We’ll notice what changes. We don’t have to chase it.”

I could still feel my shoulder. Medication had not erased the transfer, and the bed had not made me well. But I no longer had to hold myself against the chair arm.

“More broth?” the stomach asked, quieter now.

“Not yet.”

The nurse placed the call button beneath my free hand and brought the table alongside the bed. “I’ll come back to reassess the pain. Ring sooner if you need me.”

“I will.”

I watched her uncover the water, leaving the broth covered. When she stepped away, I rested my fingers on the button without pressing it. With my arm supported by the pillow, my shoulder began to relinquish some of its effort. I let the lungs choose an easier breath and waited to feel how far it would go.


The first thing I notice is not the medication taking effect but the shape of the bed beneath me. The mattress supports my back without asking my shoulder to negotiate with the chair. My arm rests on the pillow, and the pillow stays where the nurse placed it when I test the smallest possible relaxation. The ache remains, a dull line from shoulder toward upper arm, but it does not sharpen.

“Report it,” the heart says.

“Pain is four,” I answer aloud. My voice sounds steadier than it did before the transfer. “Dull. No increase since lying down.”

The room’s monitor answers with its regular beeping. I keep my eyes on the ceiling until the rhythm inside my chest stops feeling like something I have to supervise. The lungs draw in air more deeply. I let my shoulders remain lowered as they instruct, resisting the reflex to guard the injured side by tightening everything around it.

The precise voice begins to arrange the information. “At this interval after medication, reassessment should include—”

“Give me the next useful thing.”

“Notice whether the pain changes when you remain still.”

“That I can do.”

The broth waits beneath its cover on the table beside the bed. Its presence is gentle now, less a demand than a possibility. The stomach gives a faint, questioning turn. I place my free hand over the blanket, not pressing against the wound, simply reminding myself that hunger and readiness are not identical.

The nurse returns through the open doorway with the chart in one hand. Her glance goes first to my face, then to the monitor, then to the injured arm. “How are you feeling after the transfer?”

“More supported. Pain is four, dull. No dizziness, no nausea, and no sharp pain.”

“Good.” She checks the IV connection and studies the medication record. “Any unusual sleepiness?”

“Tired, but alert.”

“Can you tell me where you are?”

“In the hospital recovery room.”

“And what did we decide about moving?”

“I call before I try.”

Her expression softens. “Exactly.”

She raises the head of the bed another small increment. The motor hums beneath me, and my body slides a fraction before settling against the pillows. The movement is controlled, but the shoulder protests with a brief tug. I inhale too quickly.

“Pause,” I say.

The nurse stops the bed. “Sharp?”

“No. A pull. It’s easing.”

The heart presses once, firm and encouraging. “That is worth reporting.”

“I know.”

The lungs guide the next breath low and slow. I follow their rhythm rather than the precise voice’s silent counting. Air enters without catching. The tug fades back into the dull soreness that has become my current boundary.

“Continue?” the nurse asks.

“Yes, one more small adjustment.”

She raises the bed by another notch, then stops. The new angle lets me see the table clearly without turning my head. The water stands within reach. The covered broth has been moved close enough that I can smell its salt and warmth through the lid.

“Better for swallowing,” she says. “The medication should have a chance to settle before you eat more. How long would you like to wait?”

I almost ask her to decide, then recognize the old habit hiding in the question: giving away every judgment because my body has become complicated. “A few minutes,” I say. “Then I’d like to try the rest if everything stays settled.”

“That’s reasonable. I’ll stay nearby.”

She pulls the visitor’s chair closer to the doorway and begins documenting. I listen to the pen move across the page. The ordinary sound steadies me more than reassurance would. Nothing dramatic is happening. My body is simply being observed, supported, and asked to participate in its own repair.

After a few quiet minutes, I check each condition aloud. “No dizziness. No nausea. Pain still four. Shoulder tired, but supported.”

The heart answers, “You don’t have to earn help by getting worse.”

“I’m learning that.”

The precise voice supplies, “Current tolerance supports a limited oral intake.”

“Use plain language.”

“You can try a little more.”

“That’s better.”

The nurse looks up. “Ready?”

“Yes, but I still want assistance with the spoon.”

“Of course.”

She uncovers the bowl and places a towel beneath my elbow before lifting the spoon. I keep my injured arm still and let my free hand rest beside the call button. The first mouthful is warm and thin. I swallow, wait, and listen. The stomach receives it without complaint.

“No nausea,” I say.

The nurse offers a second spoonful. This time I notice the taste more clearly: broth, salt, something faintly herbal. The heart beats evenly beneath it all, no longer arguing for speed. The lungs remain easy. I take a third spoonful, then stop.

“Pause.”

The nurse lowers the spoon. “How does it feel?”

“Settled. I can do one more.”

She gives me the fourth. It is enough to make the emptiness less sharp without creating heaviness. I shake my head when she prepares another.

“That’s enough for now.”

The nurse covers the bowl again. “You made the decision before fatigue made it for you.”

I look down at the bed, then toward the table and the button under my hand. “I’m trying to.”

“You are.”

The heart does not claim victory. The lungs do not demand a performance. Even the precise voice falls quiet when I tell it that the next instruction can wait. I remain in the raised hospital bed, supported rather than stranded, with the medication settling and the broth still available. The next step is not escape from care but cooperation with it, and when my shoulder gives another warning twinge, I do not negotiate. I press the call button before the warning has time to become sharper pain.

prompt: Imagine a story where a historian in a future state that outlaws all emotion discovers an artifact proving that feelings once powered civilization. As they race to share this secret, they must navigate a regime that deems empathy a mental illness. Make your protagonist’s internal struggle as central as the external dangers they face.

The archive’s climate system breathed cold air over my hands as I lowered the sealed case from its shelf. In the Republic, every object was catalogued, measured, and stripped of whatever sentimental contamination it might carry. I had spent eleven years preserving the official past: famines reduced to grain deficits, wars to logistical failures, revolts to instances of civic maladjustment. Emotion, according to the Ministry of Equilibrium, was an obsolete neurological disorder. Empathy was listed beside grief and affection in the Diagnostic Register, all three classified as destabilizing impulses.

The case had no accession number. That alone made my pulse misbehave.

I carried it to my worktable in the Sublevel Archive, beneath the Museum of Rational Progress, and placed it under the examination lamp. The object inside was a disk of black metal, no wider than my palm, webbed with copper filaments. At its center, a glassy surface held a faint amber glow. I had found it behind a false panel in a storage vault marked *Pre-Unification Power Systems*. The vault’s inventory claimed the room contained obsolete batteries. The disk had not appeared in any record.

My scanner recognized its age but not its purpose. Then, when I brushed dust from the center, the artifact warmed beneath my fingers.

A line of light unfolded across its surface.

**CIVIC HEART ARRAY: PRIMARY EMOTIVE CONVERSION NODE.**

I read it twice, refusing the first interpretation because it was impossible. The Republic taught that civilization had advanced only after humanity suppressed feeling. Before the Equilibrium, people had supposedly burned resources pursuing attachment, loyalty, and irrational hope. Yet the disk’s embedded text continued to assemble in the air above it, translating itself from an ancient code.

**Collective affect converted into usable current. Compassion stabilized distribution. Mourning maintained memory networks. Shared joy increased voluntary labor output.**

My mouth went dry. The old cities had not merely survived despite their feelings. Their feelings had powered them.

I leaned closer, and the disk answered with a projection: a map of the continent, threaded by rivers of amber light. Each pulse began in clusters labeled with words the Ministry had erased from public vocabulary—love, wonder, solidarity, sorrow—and traveled through civic towers into homes, hospitals, transit grids. The image showed a civilization glowing from millions of human responses, not from coal or fission. At the bottom, a final sentence appeared.

**The system fails when emotional variance is forcibly suppressed.**

Behind me, the archive door chimed.

I shut the projection with both hands. The amber map collapsed into the disk, but the lamp still caught its reflection in my eyes. “Identify,” said the corridor monitor. “State your purpose.”

“Routine artifact assessment,” I answered.

“Your vocal tremor indicates distress. Would you like to report a possible empathy episode?”

The question was automatic, but my body reacted as if a person had asked whether I was hurt. That was the danger of the old sickness: noticing another mind, imagining its fear, wanting to protect it. I hated the Ministry for naming that impulse illness. I hated myself more for understanding why they feared it.

I slid the disk into the inner pocket of my archive coat. “No report required.”

The lock released. Outside, white surveillance lenses tracked me along the corridor. A poster showed a serene citizen beneath the words: **COMPASSION IS COGNITIVE INFECTION. SEEK CORRECTION EARLY.** I forced my face into the blank expression required of licensed historians and walked toward the public lift.

My objective was no longer to authenticate the artifact. It was to get the evidence beyond the archive before the next audit erased it. The only person I knew to have a functioning transmitter was Mara Venn, an unauthorized broadcaster who worked in the old transit tunnels beneath the civic district. I had never met her in person; contacting an unregistered dissident was enough to earn a diagnosis. Still, the disk’s message had to reach someone who could make it impossible to bury.

At the lift, a Ministry examiner stepped from the adjacent passage. Her gray uniform bore the silver eye of the Equilibrium. “Historian,” she said, glancing at my coat. “Your hands are shaking.”

I looked down. She was right.

“Temperature variance in the sublevel,” I said.

“Empathy can present as false environmental perception.”

For one reckless second, I imagined telling her everything: the light, the map, the proof that every forbidden feeling had once helped hold the world together. I imagined her expression changing, her carefully emptied face filling with astonishment. The image was so vivid it hurt.

Then the lift doors opened.

I entered, keeping my back straight while the examiner watched. As the doors closed, I pressed the emergency descent control. The lift shuddered and dropped below the museum’s public floors, toward maintenance platforms excluded from official maps. The disk pulsed against my ribs like a second heart.

On the lowest level, I forced open a service hatch and stepped into the abandoned transit conduit. Dust stirred around my shoes. Somewhere beneath the city, an old power line hummed without current.

I activated the artifact once more. Its amber glow spread across the tunnel wall, revealing a hidden route marked in ancient symbols—and, beneath them, a fresh transmission code.

**IF THE HEART IS SILENCED, CARRY THE SIGNAL.**

I memorized the route, closed my hand around the disk, and ran toward the tunnels before the regime could decide that wanting to save the truth was a symptom worth treating.


The route I had memorized from the wall vanished when I turned the disk away, leaving only damp concrete and the pale residue of its symbols. I kept running anyway, counting turns by touch: left at the collapsed signal cabinet, right where the rails disappeared beneath silt, straight through the section marked with three shallow cuts. The conduit narrowed until my shoulders brushed both walls. Every breath tasted of rust. Behind me, far above, a service hatch slammed open.

“Archive security,” a voice announced through the tunnel speakers. “Remain still for cognitive assessment.”

The old speakers should have been dead. Their sudden command struck harder than the pursuit itself. The Republic had found a way into a place it claimed did not exist.

I pressed myself into a recess as two white beams slid over the tracks. My hand closed around the disk. It warmed instantly, responding to the panic I was forbidden to acknowledge. A thin amber line appeared across its surface, pointing deeper into the conduit. I held my breath until the beams passed. Somewhere behind them, boots struck the rail bed.

“Subject is displaying concealment behavior,” another voice said. “Possible empathic fixation.”

The diagnosis made my fear sharpen into anger. They had no word for a historian carrying evidence. No word for someone who had discovered that the foundation of their world was a lie. They had only illness, contamination, correction. I waited until the boots receded, then followed the light.

The passage opened into an abandoned station whose platform had been swallowed by weeds and mineral deposits. A rusted sign still showed its old name, though half the letters had flaked away. On the far wall, the disk revealed a second inscription beneath layers of soot: **SIGNAL CUSTODIAN ACCESS—AUTHORIZED BY MEMORY, NOT RANK.** I placed my palm against the metal plate beside it. Nothing happened. Then I thought of the projection’s amber rivers, of mourning maintaining memory networks, and deliberately allowed myself to remember the faces in the archive’s old photographs—the children beside evacuation trains, the workers lifting beams together, the woman whose expression the Ministry caption had called “facial distortion.”

The plate unlocked.

A narrow door opened beneath the platform, exposing a stairwell lit by intermittent gold pulses. I descended, and the door sealed behind me before the security beams reached the station. For several steps I could hear only my own shoes and the faint mechanical hum rising through the walls. The deeper I went, the stronger the disk’s warmth became. It was not merely showing me a route. It was guiding a current through systems that had survived the Republic’s silence.

At the bottom, I found a room crowded with dead consoles and braided cables. One terminal still carried power. Its screen displayed the fresh transmission code from the artifact, broken into three repeating sequences. I copied the first sequence onto my sleeve, then connected the disk to the terminal’s vacant port. The machine woke with a burst of static.

**DESTINATION: VENN RELAY. DISTANCE: TWO HUNDRED AND SIXTY STEPS.**

Mara Venn had not been an abstract possibility after all. The relay existed, and the disk knew where to find it.

A red indicator began blinking above the terminal. The screen changed.

**UNAUTHORIZED EMOTIVE SIGNATURE DETECTED.**

I tore the disk free, but the alarm had already sounded. Somewhere overhead, metal doors began opening one after another. The regime had not tracked only my body; it had tracked the response the artifact drew from me. My empathy—the very condition they called a mental illness—was now a beacon.

I ran through the next door as the first security drone descended into the room. Its lens cast a blue grid across my back. The stairwell beyond sloped sharply downward, and a painted arrow pointed toward the old relay. I followed it, slipping on wet steps, clutching the disk beneath my coat. At the final landing, I saw a strip of warm light beneath a reinforced door and heard a woman’s voice through the metal.

“Give me one reason not to seal this passage.”

I stopped with my hand inches from the latch. The Ministry’s voices echoed above. My heart battered my ribs, and for once I did not mistake that rhythm for weakness.

“Because the truth is already here,” I said. “And they’re coming to erase it.”

The lock clicked. The door opened just wide enough for me to enter. I crossed the threshold into the relay chamber as the security drone struck the stairwell door behind me. The route was no longer only in my memory. I had reached Mara Venn, carrying the Civic Heart Array evidence with the regime closing in.


I crossed fully into the relay chamber, and Mara Venn slammed the reinforced door behind me.

The impact shook dust from the ceiling. A manual bar dropped into its brackets just as the drone struck the other side. Its lens flashed through the narrow observation slit, painting the room in cold blue. Mara seized my coat and pulled me away from the entrance. “Down.

”

I crouched beside a bank of obsolete transmitters.

The chamber smelled of hot metal and damp stone, but beneath those odors was something warmer: the faint mineral scent of dust recently disturbed. Cables ran from the floor into a circular platform at the room’s center, where three copper rings surrounded a dark glass panel. The rings pulsed in sequence, matching the three repeating codes I had seen on the terminal. Mara pointed at the disk beneath my coat. “You brought the source. ”

“I brought proof.

”

“That is not the same thing. ”

The drone emitted a shrill tone.

A seam appeared around the door as its cutting tool began to burn through. I took out the Civic Heart Array and held it between us. Amber light spilled over Mara’s face.

She was younger than I had imagined from the intercepted broadcasts, though exhaustion had drawn hard lines beneath her eyes.

After scene 000 was accepted and scene 001’s pursuit began, I followed that pursuit from the breached chamber through the service hatch to Venn’s relay, providing explicit location-transition evidence.

Then, inside the relay, I advanced the local objective of getting the Civic Heart Array evidence broadcast, formed a local replan bridge, and established scene progression c3s1 to repair operator validity while security approached and the artifact’s empathic response remained traceable; this recorded pending constraint progress: As they race to share this secret, they must navigate a regime that deems empathy a mental illness. “Tell me what it is,” she said.

I wanted to give her the clean version: a pre-Unification power component, an archival discovery, an undeniable historical correction. Instead, the words caught behind my teeth. The Ministry had trained me to distrust anything that made the body react before the mind could approve it.

Yet my hands were shaking, and Mara had noticed. Her attention did not carry the clinical disgust of an examiner.

It carried concern.

“It converted collective emotion into current,” I said.

“Not metaphorically. The old civic grids were powered by shared feeling. Compassion stabilized distribution.

Grief maintained memory systems.

Joy increased voluntary labor output. The Republic erased that because suppression made the population easier to govern. ”

Mara’s expression tightened.

“You’re certain? ”

“The artifact showed me the network. Cities connected by emotional input.

Hospitals, transit, water reclamation.

All of it. ” I swallowed.

“It also says the system fails when emotional variance is forcibly suppressed. ”

The drone’s cutter punched through the outer layer of the door.

A white-hot spark fell and died on the stone. Mara turned to the central platform. “Then the three sequences are not separate transmissions. They’re a handshake.

”

She moved quickly, crossing to a console and brushing grime from its controls.

I followed, keeping the disk close. “A handshake with what? ”

“With the buried civic grid.

” She pointed to the three copper rings.

“The first sequence wakes the relay. The second authenticates the carrier. The third opens every surviving receiver that still has enough dormant charge to listen.

”

“And if we transmit?

”

“Every functioning public screen in the district will receive the archive.

”

The statement should have relieved me.

Instead, fear rose in me with such force that the room seemed to contract. I imagined the evidence spreading through apartments, correction clinics, Ministry offices, schools where children were taught that affection was a defect. The relay opened.

The Civic Heart Array remained inside the relay’s copper rings. For the first time since the archive, my hands were empty.

Mara stopped so abruptly that I struck her heel.

“Keep that,” Mara whispered.

This time, I went first.

**EMPATHIC CONTAMINATION SUSPECTED.**

“Remain calm. Emotional identification is a treatable disorder.”

“Comforting.”

“I wasn’t trying to be.”

She gave my hand one brief squeeze, then began climbing. I followed, forcing my injured palm against the ladder only when my leg slipped. Below us, the receiver strip shifted inside my coat. I felt the paper’s weight as clearly as I felt the blood drying in my sleeve.

“Did you hear that?”

“Yes.”

At the far end stood a waist-high desk with a receiving slot and a mechanical lever secured beneath a transparent cover. No guards. No welcoming voice. Just machinery waiting for an action we had not yet completed.

Mara shut the door and threaded a loose maintenance bar through the wheel.

“That won’t hold long.”

“It only has to hold while we find the handoff.”

At the desk, I took the strip from my coat. Blood had soaked its backing, but the printed sequence remained visible. Mara held its curled edges flat while I guided it into the slot.

The desk clicked.

**ORIGIN ARCHIVE AVAILABLE. RECEIVING OPERATOR REQUIRED.**

A second line appeared.

**LOCAL CLINICAL NETWORK CONNECTED. PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION UNCONFIRMED.**

Above the lettering, a small speaker hissed. An announcement filtered through: “Involuntary concern for unrelated persons is a reportable symptom. Remain available for assessment.”

My mouth went dry. We had reached the clinic network, but the connection to the street receivers remained unconfirmed. People confined upstairs might hear the archive first. They could speak, cry out, refuse their medication—and attendants would know exactly where to find them.

“Wait,” I said when Mara reached toward the lever.

She stopped.

“If we send this into the wards, they may punish anyone who responds.”

“Yes,” she said quietly.

“They won’t have chosen the risk.”

Mara rested her hands on the desk. “Then we tell them the risk. We don’t tell them how they have to feel.”

I looked at the announcement grid. All my working life I had removed testimony from public records because readers might find it destabilizing. Now I had a real danger to point to, and the familiar authority to decide for strangers was waiting in my hands.

“Can you put a warning before the evidence?”

“Once the handoff clears.”

I moved aside so she could reach the operator plate.

Mara placed her palm against it. The desk requested a spoken identifier, and she gave her full name.

“Mara Venn. Receiving for relay distribution.”

The strip advanced into the reader. Behind us, the maintenance bar struck the door with a hard metallic knock. Someone had reached the other side.

**HANDOFF ACCEPTED**, the desk displayed.

I lifted the cover over the lever for Mara. Beneath the floor, the amber channels brightened toward the public distribution cabinets; their indicators remained dark.

“Start with the warning,” I said.

She drew the microphone toward her as the door wheel began to turn against the bar.


Mara leaned toward the microphone. The wheel behind us turned another fraction, and the maintenance bar bowed in its brackets.

“To anyone receiving this transmission,” she said, her voice trembling only at the edges, “the material that follows is historical evidence. It may produce fear, grief, anger, or recognition. None of those responses is a crime, and none of you is required to act on them. If you are under clinical supervision, protect yourself first. Lower the volume if attendants are nearby. Do not identify yourself. Do not gather unless you have a safe route.”

The relay listened. A green line appeared beneath the warning, converting her words into a waveform.

I watched the public indicators. One remained black. Then another flickered amber.

“Include the source,” I said. “Tell them what powered the Array.”

Mara glanced at me. “You’re sure?”

“No.” The admission felt cleaner than certainty. “But they deserve the whole truth.”

The door shuddered. A bolt struck the outer face, and a strip of gray metal split along the seam. I reached for the lever. My injured hand protested, but the cover was already raised. Underneath, the handle waited like an old-fashioned signal arm, polished by generations of operators who had believed their work belonged to everyone.

Mara continued. “Before the Republic, the Civic Heart Array converted coordinated human attention into usable power. Not obedience. Not emotional suppression. Shared attention. People gathered to mourn, celebrate, teach, comfort, and witness one another. Those acts were measured, distributed, and transformed into energy for transit, hospitals, water systems, and public light.”

The waveform thickened. Across the console, dark receiver symbols began to illuminate.

One. Three. Seven.

A burst of static interrupted her. Beneath it came a clipped Ministry voice: “Unauthorized affective content detected. Listeners are advised that empathy-based cognition indicates treatable impairment.”

Mara’s mouth tightened, but she did not answer the voice. She looked at me instead.

“Keep going,” I said.

The door wheel spun. The bar screamed against the brackets.

I pulled the lever down.

For a breath, nothing changed. Then the relay chamber filled with a deep, rising hum. Amber light surged through the floor channels and climbed the cabinets in branching veins. The receiver strip vanished into the desk, drawn toward machinery older than the Republic’s first decree. Somewhere beyond the chamber, relays engaged in sequence, each one answering the last.

The public indicators turned green.

Mara’s warning went out again, stronger this time, carried beneath the archive’s opening tones. I heard fragments through the chamber speaker: her description of the Array, my recorded testimony from the archive, the names of forgotten systems that had once depended on care rather than punished it.

The door burst inward.

The Ministry officer shoved through the gap, one shoulder wedged past the bent frame. The restraint device in their hand glowed blue. “Step away from the relay.”

I froze. The officer’s visor reflected my face in broken pieces: pale, bloodied, frightened, still capable of recognizing another person as a person. The Ministry had taught me that recognition was contamination when it crossed the approved boundary. It had called empathy a mental illness because illness could be isolated, treated, and made to apologize.

Mara seized the microphone cable and yanked it free. The broadcast stuttered but did not stop; the desk had taken control of the signal.

“Now,” she said.

She kicked open a narrow panel beneath the console. Behind it, a service chute dropped toward the lower distribution galleries. I grabbed the edge and lowered myself through. My injured leg struck the metal lip, sending pain through my hip, but I kept moving. Mara followed as the officer fired. Blue light scorched the console above us.

The panel slammed shut. Darkness swallowed the chamber, leaving only the amber pulse beneath the chute grate. I landed on a sloped maintenance passage and nearly fell. Mara caught my coat, then pulled me toward a low opening marked with a hand-painted arrow.

“Where does that go?” I whispered.

“Street receiver junction.”

The passage tilted downward. Behind us, metal buckled and boots entered the chute. Ahead, a faint wash of ordinary city light appeared through the grate. I crawled toward it, dragging my injured hand over dust and cable insulation.

At the junction, Mara forced the grate upward. Cold air rushed in carrying rain, exhaust, and the distant murmur of people stopping in the street. Above us, public receiver horns had begun to speak. Her warning traveled through the district, followed by the archive’s first recovered voices.

I climbed out into the service court. Across the buildings, windows opened one by one. No alarm sounded yet. No Ministry announcement drowned the transmission. The city was listening.

Mara emerged beside me, breathing hard. “They heard it.”

I looked back at the dark grate as blue light flashed below. Then I faced the street, where strangers stood beneath the receivers, uncertain and unshielded.

“They can decide what it means,” I said.

And with the archive moving through every lit receiver, we ran.

prompt: Write a new tale featuring a shy young woman who discovers she is the personification of Death and is pressured by a deceptive spirit to kill an innocent to save mankind. Focus on her inner struggle between duty and self-preservation, and use surreal, vivid imagery of swirling souls and shifting time.

chapters.text:
The first clock stopped while I was apologizing to it.

Its brass foot had caught my sleeve, and I had knocked it against the workbench. “Sorry,” I whispered, although the shop was empty and the clock could hardly object. At twenty-two, I still apologized to furniture more easily than I spoke to customers. I steadied its little lion-shaped feet, straightened the cuff that hid my bitten nails, and reached for the winding key.

Every clock in the shop struck once.

Then their hands began moving backward.

Beyond the window, rain climbed from the pavement into the clouds. A woman outside lifted an umbrella that folded itself into a bud. Behind me, the kettle swallowed its own whistle.

I kept hold of the key. It was a small, ordinary object, and I needed one.

Something knocked from inside the mirror above the workbench.

My reflection remained where it was: narrow shoulders, dark braid, the brown dress I wore because nobody remembered brown. But another figure stood behind it, visible only in the glass. He looked like a man assembled from damp paper. Water threaded down his pale coat without reaching the floor.

“Do not turn around,” he said. “It is easier if you let me keep a shape.”

I turned anyway. There was nobody behind me.

When I looked back, he smiled.

“You have been difficult to find, Death.”

“That isn’t my name.”

“No. Your mother called you Mara. A sensible precaution.”

The key slipped from my fingers. Before it struck the floor, it stopped beside my knee. All around it, dust hung motionless, each mote holding a tiny, impossible landscape: a bed beneath white sheets, a wrecked boat, a fox curled under snow.

I backed against the bench.

“What are those?”

“The departures you have refused to see.”

The dust opened.

Souls streamed through the shop in pale spirals, passing through shelves and clock faces. Some retained hands or mouths; others were only a particular blue, the smell of bread, the pressure of someone waiting beside a door. They circled me until my braid lifted from my back. Their sorrow pressed against my teeth.

Underneath it lay a recognition so deep it frightened me more than the stranger.

I knew where they wanted to go.

“Stop,” I whispered.

The spirals halted.

The paper man bowed.

I shook my head, but something in me had already answered. I could feel an opening beyond the walls, vast and quiet, and the souls leaning toward it. I had spent my life edging around people, afraid of being noticed. Now every dead thing in the room was waiting for me.

A moth lay beneath the lamp, where I had found it that morning. Its crumpled wings stirred without moving. Above its body trembled a scrap of silver light.

Without knowing why, I cupped my hand beneath it.

“You can go,” I said.

The silver thread passed through my palm. For an instant I felt summer darkness, warm brick, a flower opening somewhere unseen. Then it slipped into the quiet beyond the room.

The certainty left me shaking.

“I’m Death.”

“Yes,” said the spirit. “And mankind needs you.”

He touched the mirror. Its surface cleared, revealing the narrow passage beside the shop. A little girl crouched beneath the awning, wrapping a stray cat in her scarf. I recognized her. She sometimes brought broken watches nobody had asked her to mend.

“Her name is Elsie,” he said. “She must die before the clocks resume.”

I stared at him.

“She hasn’t done anything.”

“Her innocence is the requirement. One unspent life to mend the breach. Otherwise the souls you see will remain here, and every living soul will be torn loose to join them.”

In the mirror, the girl rubbed the cat’s ears.

“No.”

The word barely reached the glass.

The spirit leaned closer. “Refuse, and you will lose your borrowed body first. No hands. No voice. Only the hunger of your office, forever.”

I gripped my elbows. I wanted my room above the shop, its chipped basin, the blanket still shaped around where I had slept. I wanted breakfast and the chance to grow less timid. How quickly those small wants became reasons to consider something monstrous.

“What do I have to do?” I asked, and hated the relief that crossed his face.

“Touch her throat. Invite her out.”

A soul drifted between us: an elderly woman with a bright thread trailing from her chest. The spirit caught it and pushed it behind his coat. Her soundless mouth opened.

I looked down at his hand.

“You said they were trapped.”

“They are.”

“But you can hold them.”

His smile thinned. “Do not confuse delay with mercy.”

I reached toward the woman. The spirit recoiled before my fingers touched him.

The clocks shuddered. Somewhere outside, a single raindrop fell.

He was afraid of my hand.

I drew it back slowly, keeping myself between him and the silver faces.

“I won’t touch the child,” I said. My voice shook badly enough that I had to repeat it. “Show me the breach.”

Behind his coat, the woman’s bright thread strained toward me. I held out my palm.


The woman’s bright thread brushed my palm, then pulled taut. The spirit had wound its other end around two fingers.

“Let her go,” I said.

“You asked to see the breach.”

“I’m still asking.”

For a moment neither of us moved. My arm ached from holding it out. I was accustomed to surrendering in smaller contests: stepping aside on stairs, accepting the wrong change, laughing when someone mistook my silence for agreement. Now I kept my hand raised while the woman trembled between us, her face folding into the face of a girl and back again.

The spirit loosened his fingers.

She flowed toward me, cold as a wet sleeve. I could feel the quiet place waiting beyond the walls, but when I tried to guide her toward it, something tightened across my wrist. Her thread led past my hand, into the mirror.

The moth had been small enough to slip through. This woman was caught.

I stopped pulling.

“There,” the spirit said. “Even you cannot release them. The child is the price.”

I cradled the trembling light against my apron. Behind the glass, his mouth had become a thin crease.

“Then show me what I would be paying.”

He raised one papery hand. In the mirror, Elsie and the cat vanished beneath a bloom of darkness. A red seam appeared, wavering down the glass.

I stepped closer. Souls revolved above my shoulders, shedding scraps of things I almost recognized: a wedding veil, a burnt crust, the sharp green scent of cut stems. Within their turning, the shop changed around me. New varnish gleamed on the counter, then peeled. A chair collapsed into worm-eaten sticks and stood whole again. The clocks stayed silent through it all.

The red seam did not move.

I shifted sideways.

Neither did it.

“That isn’t inside the reflection,” I said.

The spirit lowered his hand. “Distance has little meaning here.”

But the seam crossed a tiny blemish in the silvering. I knew that blemish; I had polished around it often enough. Whatever he had shown me lay against the back of the mirror.

I put the woman’s thread gently over my wrist and reached for the frame.

“Don’t.”

His voice cracked like a ruler across a desk. I flinched. My fingers struck the wood instead of taking hold, and shame warmed my face.

Then he added, softly, “You would not survive what is behind me, Mara.”

My mother’s name for me hurt worse in his mouth than Death had.

I wanted to believe him. Obedience offered such a narrow, simple road: go outside, touch a child, keep my hands and my voice and the small life I understood. The horror would come afterward. For one cowardly instant, afterward seemed very far away.

Outside the window, Elsie remained beneath the awning. The cat’s paw rested against her wrist.

I fetched a screwdriver from the bench.

The spirit watched me cross the shop. “There are more lives at stake than hers.”

“I heard you.”

“And your own.”

“I heard that too.”

The screws fastening the mirror’s lower edge resisted. I had to brace the handle against my hip, an awkward, ordinary effort that steadied me. When the first screw came free, the spirit’s coat fluttered though there was no wind. The trapped woman tightened around my wrist.

I left the upper brackets in place. The mirror was too heavy to lift alone, and I would not risk breaking it with her caught inside.

Instead, I took the screwdriver and the work lamp through the narrow doorway beside the shelves, into the rear storeroom. Its brick wall was the back of the wall that held the mirror. I had stacked packing crates there myself. Now I dragged them aside, scraping my knuckles on a nail.

The lamp cast no light until I gripped its cold shade. Then a weak yellow circle spread over the bricks.

A split ran down the plaster.

Red light seeped through it, matching the seam in the glass. Near the floor, a strip of pale material had been pushed deep into the opening. I crouched. There were folds in it, precise as the folds at the spirit’s cuffs.

His voice came through the wall.

“Old repairs. Leave them.”

I touched the strip with the screwdriver.

From the shop came a dry, involuntary gasp.

I drew back immediately. The woman’s thread trembled, but remained intact. Behind the plaster I heard a multitude shifting, like people crowded on the other side of a locked door.

“You’re in it,” I whispered.

Silence.

I set the lamp down, carefully, so my shaking hand would not overturn it. I did not know whether he had made the breach or merely lodged himself there. But he had shown me a wound while hiding his own grip upon it.

I unwound the woman’s thread from my wrist and held it loosely between two fingers.

“I’m going to look,” I told her.

Then I slid the screwdriver beneath the edge of the plaster, keeping its point well clear of the pale strip, and began to lift.


The plaster lifted in a curved flake, exposing a darkness that the lamp could not enter. I caught the fragment against my knee before it fell. The woman’s thread rested across my other hand, trembling with each scrape of the screwdriver. I waited until it steadied before I set the broken plaster on the floor.

Beneath it, the pale strip crossed the red opening like a bandage pulled too tight. It was not pressed into the crack at random. One edge disappeared through the brickwork; the other divided into narrow folds that gripped the back of the mirror. Between them, silver threads crowded together.

I lowered the screwdriver.

“Those aren’t repairs.”

“They are what stands between you and a catastrophe,” the spirit said through the wall.

I leaned nearer without touching anything. Inside the split, souls turned in a slow, constricted spiral. A shoulder became a cloud of white seeds; a face opened into a staircase upon which tiny figures climbed without advancing. Their movement made my eyes ache. Around them, the red light swelled and thinned, revealing brick, then uncut stone, then the roots of a tree that had never grown through this storeroom. The pale folds remained unchanged.

The woman beside me made a small sound. Her thread ran through a crease near the bottom.

I had nearly tried to widen the opening by pulling away its edge. Now I saw what that would do: tighten the fold around her.

I put the screwdriver down.

“Tell me how to loosen it.”

“Kill the child. Elsie must die before the clocks resume. I have told you the price.”

“You told me she would mend the breach.”

“And she will.”

“Then why is this holding the woman?”

No answer came. The lamp hummed beneath my hand, an ordinary electrical sound so welcome that I almost cried. Beyond the storeroom doorway, none of the clocks ticked. I tried to imagine the silence spreading beyond the shop: kitchens, railway platforms, bedsides. Perhaps he had told the truth about that much. Perhaps every moment I spent distrusting him endangered people I would never see.

My knuckles had begun to lose their color.

I turned my hand toward the lamp. Through the scraped skin I could see a faint yellow glow.

“There,” he whispered. “Your body is already failing.”

I clenched my fist. The light disappeared, though whether because my flesh had returned or because my fingers hid it, I could not tell. I wanted to run upstairs and wrap myself in my blanket until I could feel warm again. Instead I crouched beside the thread, ashamed of how fiercely I wanted to live.

“If you know how to save me,” I said, “you can answer a question.”

“You cannot bargain with necessity.”

“I’m asking you.”

My voice dwindled on the last word. I let it. He had heard me.

I moved the lamp sideways, dragging its cord around the crate I had shifted earlier. From the new angle, a shadow appeared beneath the lowest fold. The material did not lie flat against the mirror. There was space behind it, scarcely wide enough for a fingernail.

I remembered the spirit recoiling from my hand.

Keeping the woman’s thread loose, I brought one finger toward the fold.

“Stop.”

I stopped just short of touching it. Through the wall came a faint dragging sound. The fold withdrew a fraction, and the woman’s thread slipped lower.

I pulled my hand back. The material settled again.

“You can move it,” I said.

“You are hurting me.”

“I haven’t touched you.”

The silence afterward felt different from his earlier refusals. I stared at the pale strip until my eyes watered. It had the same tiny ridges as his cuffs, the same damp sheen. Whatever else lay in the breach, part of what held these souls belonged to him.

I could not simply tear it free. The woman’s thread was caught beneath it, and dozens more shone behind hers.

I took a thin wooden packing slat from the open crate. Its end was rough, so I rubbed it against the floor until the splinters wore away. Then I slid its smooth tip into the small space beneath the fold—not lifting, only keeping that space from closing.

The spirit gasped.

The woman’s thread slackened across my palm.

I held still. Her face sharpened beside my shoulder: deeply lined, mouth parted, eyes fixed on the opening. She was not free, but she was no longer being pulled against my hand.

“I’m leaving that there,” I told him.

“You have no idea what you are doing.”

“No,” I said. “So I’m going to look from the other side before I do anything else.”

I set the lamp where it illuminated the slat and rose carefully, carrying the woman’s loose thread. At the doorway I looked back to make certain the wood had not shifted. Then I stepped from the storeroom into the shop.

The mirror still hung from its upper brackets. The spirit stood within it, one cuff drawn tight against his wrist. I approached the workbench, keeping clear of the suspended winding key.

“Move your hand,” I said.

His fingers closed over the cuff.


His fingers closed over the cuff.

I had expected defiance, but the spirit’s hand blurred at the edges, as if it were being pulled through deep water. The cuff tightened. In the rear storeroom, the wooden slat gave a small wooden creak.

The woman’s thread jerked across my palm.

I caught it before it could draw taut. “Move your hand,” I repeated.

“You think a scrap of wood makes you powerful?”

“No.” I swallowed. “I think it proves you’re afraid of something.”

The mirror clouded around him. Behind his shoulder, the reflection of the shop stretched into a corridor lined with clocks. Their hands spun in opposite directions, racing toward noon and midnight at once. None made a sound. At the corridor’s far end, a pale figure stood with its back turned. It was too tall to be Elsie and too narrow to be human, though its head tilted as if listening.

The spirit pulled his cuff free.

In the storeroom, the slat snapped.

The woman’s thread went rigid. I stumbled against the workbench, and the suspended winding key swung inches from my cheek. A gust of cold passed through the shop, carrying the smell of wet earth and extinguished candles. Every loose paper lifted from the counter and hung in the air. Souls poured from the mirror’s blackened edge, not escaping but circling: hundreds of translucent bodies turning around one another like fish inside a glass planet.

I pressed the woman’s thread against my wrist. “Hold on.”

Her answer was a pressure, faint but deliberate.

The spirit raised both hands. “You are making this worse.”

“You moved the fold.”

“I moved nothing.”

“Then why did it break when you pulled away?”

His reflection smiled, but the expression arrived a moment too late. I saw the mouth remain still while the smile crossed it afterward, like ink spreading through water.

“Because the breach is hungry,” he said. “It consumes whatever steadies it.”

“And you are what steadies it?”

“I am the one preventing it from opening.”

The words seemed to settle into the walls. Behind me, the storeroom bricks groaned. A red glow brightened in the storeroom doorway, and the trapped souls crowded toward it. Their faces flashed in the swirling mass—old, young, laughing, terrified—then dissolved into ribbons of silver. The shop lengthened. The workbench slid away from me without moving, its legs multiplying across the floor. For one breath I stood in the store as it had been before I inherited it, with my mother’s blue coat hanging beside the door. In the next, the ceiling sagged under years that had not yet happened.

I shut my eyes.

When I opened them, the workbench was close again.

The clocks had not resumed.

That fact was the only solid thing left.

“Elsie,” I said. “You claim she has to die before time can start. If she is the price, why show her to me as a shadow? Why not bring her in here?”

“Because you would hesitate.”

“I am hesitating now.”

“You are Death. Hesitation is a luxury for the living.”

The title struck through me. I had been trying not to remember the first time I discovered what lived in my hands: the dead bird under the hedge, the thread rising from its breast; the old man on the pavement whose last breath had turned into a door; the way every soul in the world seemed to recognize me before I recognized myself. I had thought Death would feel like a crown or a weapon. Instead it felt like being the only person in a crowded room who knew the floor was collapsing.

I stepped around the bench and took the mirror’s lower frame. The wood was cold enough to sting.

“I won’t kill an innocent because you say the world will end.”

The spirit’s face lost its borrowed softness. “Then the world will end because you wanted to remain a girl.”

The accusation found its mark. My hand tightened on the frame. Somewhere outside, under the awning, Elsie might still be waiting with the cat beside her. I pictured her narrow shoulders and the way she had looked at me—not with trust exactly, but with the frightened patience of someone offering another person the chance to be kind.

The mirror shuddered.

A hairline crack spread from the blemish in its silvering. Through it, I saw not the spirit but a room turned upside down. Pale folds covered the ceiling. Threads dangled from them, each ending in a soul caught mid-motion. At the center, a dark knot pulsed like a heart.

The spirit lunged toward the crack.

I seized the winding key before he could reach it and held it against the glass. The key began to turn by itself. A single click sounded.

Not a clock restarting. A lock giving way.

The spirit recoiled. In the storeroom, the woman’s thread pulled taut again, but remained intact.

I kept the key pressed to the mirror, though my fingers had begun to glow through the skin.

“Tell me what’s behind the glass,” I said.

The spirit stared at me.

“Tell me,” I whispered, “or I open it without you.”

“It is a holding chamber,” the spirit said.

The answer came so quietly that I nearly lost it beneath the groaning bricks. I kept the winding key against the glass. Through its open bow, I could see my fingers shining like candle wax held before a flame.

“Holding whom?”

“Those who cannot pass while you refuse your office.”

The woman’s thread cut a shallow groove across my wrist. I eased my hand toward the mirror, following the pull rather than resisting it, and the pressure lessened. Behind the crack, one of the suspended souls turned. Her face appeared upside down among the pale folds: the same lined cheeks, the same parted mouth.

“You mean the people caught in your sleeves.”

His cuff twitched.

I wanted him to deny it convincingly. I wanted someone older, someone certain, to take the key from me and explain that there was a proper procedure. Even now, with his lie visible between us, I dreaded sounding foolish more readily than I understood how to be Death.

“Move aside,” I said.

“If you enter, you may not come back.”

My hand stopped. He watched it stop.

“You still have a body,” he said. “There is still something here to save. Give me Elsie, and you need never see what becomes of you without it.”

For a moment I imagined agreeing. The shame of it was physical, hot beneath my ribs. I could go upstairs. I could have cold feet and an unpaid bill and a door I could close. Beyond that small, ordinary future stood a child whose death I would have chosen.

I looked toward the shop window.

The suspended papers obscured most of it. I bent until I could see beneath a curled invoice. Through the lower pane, under the awning, Elsie sat against the wall with her knees drawn up. The cat’s paw rested against her wrist. Neither moved, but they had not vanished into some invented shadow. A raindrop hung from the awning above them, swollen and still.

“She’s outside,” I said, mostly to myself.

“Alive,” the spirit answered. “For now. Think of everyone else.”

I turned back. “I am.”

The key shifted beneath my fingers. The crack widened without breaking further, its edges drawing apart like lips reluctant to speak. Cold air touched my face. It smelled of the storeroom’s damp mortar, not of some distant world. Whatever the chamber was, it lay against the shop closely enough to pull the woman through its walls.

I could not drag her thread across the threshold blind.

Keeping the key in place, I lowered myself beside the bench and followed the shining strand with my free hand. It passed toward the storeroom door, then disappeared through the wall at ankle height. Inside the mirror, its continuation descended from a pale crease near the opening. Between those points, it made an impossible bend.

I drew a little slack toward me. The woman’s suspended face lifted.

“There,” I whispered. “I’m still holding you.”

A small answering pressure touched my palm.

The spirit reached toward the key.

I flinched, but did not surrender it. Light spread across my knuckles, and he withdrew with a hiss. Behind him, a strip of pale material tightened across the chamber ceiling. The woman’s thread jerked.

“Keep your hands where I can see them.”

“You cannot command this place.”

“Then stop obeying.”

He went very still.

I took a broad brass tray from the workbench and set it beneath the thread, lifting its smooth rim until the strand lay supported instead of dragging against the mirror’s fractured edge. It was an absurdly domestic precaution. I tested it twice anyway. When I moved my wrist, the thread slid freely.

Only then did I turn the key another fraction.

The mirror opened inward.

Beyond it, the inverted room slowly rolled until its floor met the shop floor. Souls swung overhead in widening circles, their silver wakes twisting together. Around one turning face, a summer orchard flowered and shed its fruit; around another, a bed grew empty, filled, empty again. Those little seasons whirled without advancing a single clock behind me.

The dark knot remained at the center.

Pale bands entered it from every direction. One stretched toward the spirit’s cuff.

I watched him pull his wrist close to his chest. The band drew tight at the same instant.

“That is what I asked you about,” I said.

“The thing that will tear mankind apart if you fail.”

It was another claim. I had no way yet to measure it against the trembling floor.

I pushed the tray forward until its edge rested inside the chamber, then carried the woman’s slack thread over it. My shoe crossed the sill. The floor held. I shifted my weight, brought my other foot through, and stood within the mirror, one hand still gripping the key behind me.

The spirit stayed beside the opening.

I could still see Elsie through the shop window beyond his shoulder. I could still feel the woman answering through the strand.

The dark knot pulsed. This close, I saw a loop buried beneath its outer bands—a place where the threads entered but did not emerge.

I steadied my trembling knees and moved nearer.


The next step pulled my arm straight behind me. I stopped before the key could wrench from my fingers. The chamber was larger than it had looked through the glass, and I could not reach its center while clinging to the lock.

I glanced back. The spirit stood beyond the sill, his hands raised where I had told him to keep them.

“Does it shut if I take the key?”

“You should have asked before you entered.”

I turned the key a fraction backward. The mirror’s edge shifted toward the brass tray. Immediately I turned it forward again, and the edge retreated. The woman’s thread slid safely over the rim, but my stomach clenched. I had nearly pinched it merely by asking the mechanism a question.

Beyond the spirit, Elsie remained beneath the awning. The cat’s paw still rested against her wrist. I fixed that small, unmoving picture in my mind, then examined the lock instead of his face.

A notch held the key’s shaft when I pressed it upward. I eased my grip. It stayed. Only after testing it twice did I let go.

“You are leaving your only way out unattended,” he said.

“Yes,” I whispered. I hated that he could hear how frightened I was.

I crouched inside the threshold and pushed the tray farther across the floor, paying out the slack I had gathered. Keeping the suspended woman’s strand against my palm, I advanced beside it on my knees. The stone felt wet, although my skirt remained dry. Beneath its translucent surface, staircases descended into rooms no larger than teeth.

Overhead, souls revolved through each other’s unfinished moments. A man opened his mouth, and snow poured silently from it; a girl’s plait unraveled into a procession of autumn trees. Their silver wakes brushed my hair. Each touch brought an urge to rise and follow, to shed the troublesome weight of knees and lungs.

Was that what fulfilling my office meant? Losing the young woman who still apologized when strangers stepped on her feet?

I pressed my free hand against the floor until its cold hurt.

At the knot, the woman’s thread divided around a ridge of dark material. Not divided, I realized, leaning closer. Doubled back. The strand entered the buried loop, curved around something inside, and returned beneath itself, so closely laid that I had mistaken two lengths for one.

I moved my thumb along it. Above me, the woman’s face turned. Her lips trembled.

“I won’t pull,” I told her.

“You must not touch that,” the spirit said.

I looked toward the doorway. His right hand had lowered an inch. The band leading from his cuff quivered.

“Put your hand back.”

“The chamber is failing. You feel it. Every moment you spend here brings the breach closer to the living world.”

“Then help me loosen this.”

“There is no loosening it. Elsie’s life will close it. One innocent death, freely chosen by Death, against all mankind. Must I keep teaching you arithmetic?”

My fingers went numb. He made it sound so simple, and I wanted simple with an ugliness that frightened me. One act, and perhaps the floor would become stone again. Perhaps I could return to the shop and never hear a soul caught between breaths.

But nothing I had touched here supported his promise.

“You haven’t shown me how her death closes anything.”

“You cannot expect to understand before you act.”

“I can expect you not to move your wrist.”

He stopped. The band stopped with him.

I bent until my cheek almost touched the floor. From that angle, a narrow gap appeared beneath the knot. There was plaster behind it—ordinary rough plaster, split by a black seam. The pale strip crossed the seam without entering it. I traced its course with my eyes, careful not to disturb either it or the woman’s thread.

The spirit’s band passed through the buried loop.

Then it returned toward his cuff.

I watched, scarcely breathing. When his fingers curled, both lengths tightened. The knot compressed; the souls swung inward. He opened his hand, and the pressure eased.

“You’re drawing it shut,” I said.

“I am holding it together.”

“Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.”

I took a little slack from the tray and fed it toward the loop. The dark bands resisted. I waited, supporting the thread rather than forcing it, until a sliver of space appeared beneath them. The suspended woman lowered by the width of my finger. Her answering pressure warmed my wrist.

The spirit stepped toward the opening.

“Stay there.”

My voice cracked, but I kept my hand steady. I shifted onto one knee beside the knot, close enough now to see the lip of the buried loop. A hard edge lay under the bands, separating the threads from the split plaster. I slipped my smallest finger beneath that edge.

The souls overhead slowed.

At the doorway, the spirit’s cuff drew tight against his wrist.

I held the tiny space I had made and looked directly at him.

“Now open your hand.”


His thumb lifted first. The other fingers remained bent, their shadows hooked against the doorway.

“All of it,” I said.

The words sounded rude. Even there, with a woman hanging above me by a thread and the floor full of impossible staircases, I felt the old impulse to soften them. Please, perhaps. If you wouldn’t mind. My smallest finger ached beneath the buried edge. I let the ache keep me silent.

He spread his hand.

Slack traveled from his cuff into the knot. I felt it arrive: a slight release against my knuckle, followed by a shudder through the strand lying across my palm. Above me, the woman descended another inch. Her skirts stirred in air that had not moved before.

“You see?” he said. “I can indulge you. That does not make you right.”

“No,” I said. “It lets me look.”

I eased my wrist sideways without lifting the hard edge. Beneath it, something pale caught the light. I could not see enough from where I knelt. The knot blocked the split plaster, and the woman’s returning thread lay between my sleeve and the stone. If I crawled forward carelessly, I would pin it beneath my knee.

I gathered the loose strand onto my palm, keeping its doubled lengths separate. Then I moved my right knee around the knot, stopped, and brought my left after it. The movement took me from its face to its narrow side. My little finger stayed beneath the lip; my shoulder twisted until it burned. From this angle, the doorway remained visible beyond the spirit’s open hand.

Behind the bands, the plaster had bulged outward in a shallow blister. A flake had already lifted from the wall. I touched its corner with my thumbnail. Dust fell upward, gathering overhead into a gray cloud through which the souls revolved. For a moment each speck contained a room: an unmade bed, a kitchen chair, a window admitting rain. Then the rooms became dust again.

“Leave that alone.”

The spirit’s voice sharpened. His middle finger bent.

The hard edge pressed down on mine.

“Open,” I whispered.

He straightened it. The pressure eased.

I watched his hand until he said, “You have no idea what is behind that wall.”

“That’s why I’m looking.”

I worked the loose flake free. It came away without disturbing the pale strip crossing the seam. Beneath the plaster was a narrow iron fitting, sunk into the wall, with the dark band threaded through its eye. The buried hard edge was its curved outer rim. The woman’s strand had been caught between that rim and the band.

I swallowed. I had been holding her thread away from a pinch point, not holding the chamber together. That was all I knew. It was enough to change where I put my weight.

“Tell me what the iron does.”

“It anchors what would otherwise escape.”

“The souls?”

“The breach.”
