Its feet complain against the floor, and for an instant I brace for an answering scrape from the corridor. Nothing comes. I switch off the desk lamp and step over the chair leg holding the door. Mara waits while I remove it, set it inside, and pull the office door shut.

We pass the radiator. The hooked metal remains on the high shelf, an ordinary piece of rubbish now that I know how it moved. I shine the flashlight beneath it once, then turn toward the stairs.

At the first landing, I stop.

Mara is two steps below me. “What?”

“I heard him say it.”

She waits.

“That he wanted me to have my own life.” I grip the rail; its paint feels gritty. “I heard him. I’m not pretending I didn’t.”

“You don’t have to prove that to me.”

“I think I’m proving it to myself.”

His reassurance is still there, unmistakable in his voice. It has not made me feel better in the uncomplicated way I expected truth to work. Instead it has made some of my oldest explanations difficult to repeat. I start climbing again before I can turn that difficulty into another reason to stay underground.

Outside, the air cools the sweat beneath my collar. Mara puts away the flashlight. We walk toward the house with enough space between us for another person, although neither of us steps aside when the pavement narrows.

“I wish you’d let me be angry then,” I say.

She turns her head.

“When he asked you to wait. Or afterward. I could have been angry with him. We could have had that.”

“I kept putting it off,” she says. “After a while, giving you the tape also meant telling you how long I’d had it.”

I look at her. She keeps walking, her hands down by her sides.

“That’s not an excuse,” she adds.

“No,” I say. “It isn’t.”

For several paces, our shoes are the only sound. I feel no satisfaction in having made her admit it. But I am glad the words are outside me now, where she has to hear them too.

At the house, I fumble the key twice. Mara does not offer to take it. Inside, I leave my coat on and climb the stairs, then pull down the attic steps. The hinges give their familiar complaint. I go up first, carrying the cassette in my hand so it cannot bend against my ribs.

The leather-bound book is where I hid it. I kneel and draw it out. Dust catches in the creases of the cover. From below, Mara asks whether she should stay downstairs.

“On the steps,” I say. “Please.”

Her weight settles on a lower tread. I can see one hand on the rail, but not her face.

I open the book and search for the hospital entry, turning carefully, unwilling now to skim the surrounding regrets as though they are unimportant. When I find it, I hold the page flat with both hands.

I read it once. Then again, more slowly.

On a loose scrap beside the book, I write: *What happened?* Beneath that: *What did I decide it meant?*

The eraser rests in my pocket. I leave it there.

I place the cassette across the scrap to keep it from curling and bend closer to the page. Before I choose anything, I am going to answer both questions.


The entry is shorter than I remember.

*I left his room before he woke. He asked me to go. I said I would come back. I did not. I have carried the leaving as if it were the whole event.*

Below it, in darker ink, I have added a sentence at some later point, the letters pressed so hard they have cut into the paper.

*He died while I was gone.*

I touch the groove beneath the words. The statement is true, but it has always stood in my mind as if it were a verdict. I read the entry again, looking for the part I have omitted by refusing to look directly at it. There is no mention of the nurse who came into the hall, no mention of the call I ignored because I was standing outside the hospital with my hands shaking. There is no mention of his request.

Mara shifts on the stair below. “What does it say?”

I keep my finger on the page. “That I left. That he died while I was gone.”

“That’s not all of it.”

“No.” I look toward the opening in the floor, where her face is partly hidden by the attic’s shadow. “The first sentence says he asked me to go.”

She does not answer. The silence is not evasive this time. It gives the sentence room.

I turn the page back and find the hospital entry’s first version beneath the one I have been reading. The ink is faded, but I can make out the line I crossed through: *He looked relieved when I said I needed air.* Underneath, I had written, *I abandoned him because I was relieved too.*

My stomach tightens. I remember the room in pieces: the plastic cup beside his bed, the blue curtain that would not close all the way, his mouth dry from the medication. I remember asking whether he wanted me to stay. I remember him saying, “Go home, Next. Sleep.” I remember believing that permission was another form of accusation.

“I made the meaning first,” I say.

Mara’s hand tightens on the rail. “What meaning?”

“That if I wanted to leave, even for an hour, it proved I wanted him gone.” I rub my thumb over the crossed-out words. “Then when he died, I changed it to mean I had chosen wrong. Not just that I was gone. That I had chosen being gone.”

The cassette in my hand has left a rectangular warmth against my palm. I had thought the tape would tell me whether I was guilty. Instead, my brother’s voice has made the question less useful. He had known I wanted to leave. He had heard the shame in me and tried to remove it before it hardened.

“Can we listen to the rest?” Mara asks.

I glance at her. “You can stay there.”

“I will.”

I close the book, but do not put it away. I pick up the cassette, carry the book beneath one arm, and climb down from the attic onto the landing. Mara moves aside to let me pass. I go downstairs first, then cross the hall to the office where the small tape player sits beside the desk. The transition feels deliberate: not an escape from the page, but a way of placing its words beside the recording.

The cassette clicks into the machine. I press play.

Static fills the room. Then my brother’s breath, thin and uneven, comes through the speaker.

“If you’re listening to this because you found the book,” he says, “you’re probably trying to identify the exact moment you failed me. Don’t. There isn’t one.”

I grip the edge of the desk.

“I asked you to leave because I wanted you to leave. I wanted you to go home, eat something, sleep in your own bed. I was sick, not trapped, and you were not my guard.”

A small laugh catches in his throat. It is the laugh I remember from the kitchen, before the hospital took away his strength.

“You looked relieved when I told you to go. Good. You should have been relieved. Loving me didn’t require you to be afraid every minute.”

The tape warbles. I reach toward the player, then stop myself.

“I need you to understand this part. If I die while you’re gone, that won’t turn your leaving into a decision to kill me. It will mean I died while you were gone. Those are different facts. Don’t use my death to erase the difference.”

My knees weaken. I sit in the desk chair.

Mara remains by the door, close enough to hear, far enough not to touch me without permission. The voice continues, softer now.

“And if there’s something you regret more than this, choose carefully. Don’t erase the pain just because it tells you I mattered. You can keep loving me without keeping the punishment.”

The tape clicks off.

For a while I watch the reels stop turning. Then I take the eraser from my pocket and set it on the desk beside the book. I do not lift it. I write beneath the hospital entry: *I left because he asked me to. I decided it meant I had abandoned him. Those are different facts.*

The sentence does not absolve me. That is why I trust it.


The ink shines beneath the lamp. I wait for it to sink into the paper before moving my hand.

Nothing else changes. The hospital entry remains above my addition, with its crossings-out and the deep groove of the sentence about his death. My brother is still dead. His voice is on the cassette, not waiting in another room. I know this, but after hearing him speak so plainly, the silence makes me look toward the door.

Mara stands there, rubbing one thumb along the seam of her sleeve.

“Are you going to use it?” she asks.

The eraser lies beside my wrist. One corner is rounded; another looks sharp enough to lift a single letter. I pick it up. It weighs almost nothing.

“I thought I could choose the worst one,” I say. “Then I thought I could choose the least dangerous one. Something small enough that losing it wouldn’t matter.”

“And now?”

“Now I don’t believe I know what losing it means.”

I hold it above the sentence I have just written. There is a precise temptation here: not to change the night, not to bring him back, but to remove the conviction that I abandoned him. I can almost imagine waking without that familiar argument already underway.

Then I look at my handwriting. I have spent years making his request mean its opposite. The recording has given me something with which to challenge that. I have barely begun.

“If I rub this out,” I say, “I won’t know whether I’ve stopped believing it or just lost the ability to question it.”

Mara pulls out the other chair, then pauses.

“Yes,” I tell her.

She sits. The desk remains between us.

“I can’t tell you it would be safe,” she says.

“I’m not asking you to.”

“I know.”

I put the eraser down. My fingers leave a damp mark on its pale surface.

The choice feels disappointingly physical. There ought to be some unmistakable sensation when I turn away from the thing I have wanted this badly. Instead, my shoulders ache. I am hungry. Part of me is still making a case for trying one word.

“I’m keeping the entry,” I say. “All of it. Including what I wrote tonight.”

Mara looks down at the page. “You can change your mind.”

“Yes.” I draw the book toward me. “But I don’t want to spend every bad night deciding again.”

I find an empty envelope in the desk drawer and slide the eraser inside. Across the front I write what it promises, followed by what I do not know: whether it changes memory, feeling, events, or anything that belongs to someone else. I fold the flap without sealing it.

“Will you keep that away from the book?” I ask. “Somewhere I can’t reach for it without asking you.”

She studies the envelope before accepting it.

“I can do that.”

“This doesn’t make us all right.”

Her hand stops halfway across the desk. “I understand.”

“I need you to tell me things even when telling me makes you look bad. Especially then.”

She sets the envelope in her lap. “I should have given you the tape.”

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

I nod. I hear the apology without trying to turn it into either forgiveness or another charge against her. There will be more to say. Tonight, I have managed to say what I need.

I close the leather cover, leaving my scrap of questions between the pages. Then I lift the cassette from the player and turn it over. On the other side, beneath a rubbed patch of ink, I can make out two words: *first version*.

“The song?” I ask.

Mara leans forward to see. “Yes.”

My thumb catches against the cracked hinge of the case. I have been pursuing explanations so hard that I nearly put the music away unheard.

“Not in here,” I say.

I carry the player out of the office, with the book under my arm. Mara follows me through the hall into the kitchen. I set the book on the counter, clear two unopened envelopes from the table, and plug the player into the socket beside the kettle. The ordinary mess takes a little work to make room for us.

“Tea?” Mara asks.

“Yes, please.”

While she fills the kettle, I slip the cassette back into the player, the song side ready, and press play.

There is a scrape, a cough, then my brother counting himself in too quickly. He misses the first chord. Starts again. His voice is stronger than it is on the spoken recording, though he pushes for a note he cannot quite reach.

I laugh before I can stop myself.

Mara turns from the sink. I point at the player.

“He always blamed the guitar for that.”

“He did.”

The kettle begins its low rumble. I sit and listen through the rough opening, the unfinished line, the place where he changes his mind about the tune without stopping.

When Mara puts my cup down, I move the empty chair out with my foot.

We listen to the rest without touching the book.

prompt: Imagine a story where a disgraced young captain must negotiate a fragile peace with an alien alliance still haunted by myths of human ferocity. Focus on themes of redemption, prejudice, and how legends can shape galactic politics. Include a tense space blockade around a remote mining outpost and a secret relic that can manipulate memories.

chapters.text:
The mining outpost of Khepri’s Fall hung beneath us like a chipped tooth, its refinery lights flickering through a haze of frozen dust. Beyond it, the Veyr Alliance blockade formed a perfect crescent: twelve dark warships, their hulls ribbed with silver sails, holding position between the outpost and every available jump corridor. Their weapons were cold for now. That restraint was the only reason the miners were still alive.

I stood before the command display with my hands clasped behind my back, trying not to look at the insignia missing from my collar. The brass had stripped me of full captaincy after the Orison disaster—after I had fired on a Veyr relief vessel because its captain refused to answer my challenge. Thirty-seven aliens had died. The tribunal called it reckless aggression. The Veyr called it proof of what their oldest stories had always taught them: humans were predators who learned diplomacy only when their guns were empty.

“Another transmission,” said the comm officer.

The room fell silent as the display filled with the face of a Veyr envoy. Her features were narrow and translucent, with four black eyes set in a diamond around a pale central membrane. I had seen enough Veyr soldiers in tribunal recordings to know that her stillness was deliberate. Their diplomats performed calm the way humans performed courage.

“Captain Vale,” she said. “You have entered the cordon without authorization. Turn your vessel away, or the Alliance will enforce the quarantine.”

“My ship is carrying medical supplies and replacement oxygen membranes,” I replied. “Khepri’s Fall has six thousand civilians.”

“Your ship carries weapons.”

“Every ship carries weapons when it is frightened.”

One of her eyes contracted. “That sentiment belongs in your human war songs.”

The words struck harder than they should have. I had spent three years trying to bury the songs: tales of the Red Captains who ate enemy crews, of human fleets that pursued retreating worlds for sport, of our soldiers taking trophies from alien dead. None of them were true in the way legends were supposed to be true. A few atrocities had become a species-wide identity. My own mistake had given the stories fresh blood.

I opened the sealed authority packet from the Colonial Assembly. “I’m not here to break your blockade. I’m here to negotiate a withdrawal corridor. One shuttle at a time. Medical personnel first, then civilians too young or sick to work the mines.”

“You presume we will permit your presence.”

“No,” I said. “I’m asking you to test whether I deserve it.”

The envoy studied me through the screen. “You are the captain who destroyed the Orison envoy.”

“I am the officer who ordered the shot.”

“Your distinction is meaningless to the dead.”

I had no defense against that. Instead, I keyed the packet’s final authorization and sent it across the channel. “Then judge me by what I do here. Give me six hours aboard your flagship. Let me speak with the blockade council. If I fail, you can close the corridor and broadcast my surrender to every human settlement in the sector.”

The offer startled even me. The comm officer turned sharply, but I kept my eyes on the envoy. A public surrender would end my career, perhaps my freedom. It might also convince the Veyr that I had come to bargain rather than threaten.

The envoy’s membrane fluttered. “There is a complication, Captain Vale. Your Assembly did not send you merely to deliver supplies.”

The command display changed. A grainy image appeared: a black object half-buried beneath the mining outpost, its surface catching light in patterns that made my eyes ache. I recognized the chamber behind it. I had seen the same coordinates in the sealed packet, hidden beneath the diplomatic orders.

“The miners uncovered this beneath the oldest shaft,” she continued. “Your government knows what it is. The Alliance knows what it is. Neither wishes the other to possess it.”

I moved closer to the display. “What is it?”

“A mnemonic reliquary,” she said. “A relic from the civilization that ruled this region before either of our species reached the stars. It can remove memories. It can implant them. It can make a massacre seem like mercy and a surrender seem like treachery.”

The room seemed to contract around me. Somewhere below, six thousand miners waited beneath an alien gun line, while two governments lied about the reason for the blockade.

“And the Alliance wants it destroyed,” I said.

“No. Some within the Alliance want it destroyed. Others believe it can prove the ancient stories of human ferocity were not stories at all, but memories deliberately placed in our ancestors.”

The revelation left me cold. If the relic had shaped the Veyr’s hatred, then every negotiation between our peoples had been conducted inside someone else’s manufactured nightmare. If it could alter memory now, whoever controlled it could turn peace into a weapon.

The envoy leaned toward the transmission field. “Bring the relic to my flagship, Captain. Come unarmed, and I will open the medical corridor. Refuse, and the blockade remains.”

I looked again at the image of the buried device, then at the red icons marking the outpost’s failing oxygen reserves. “I’ll come,” I said. “But the relic leaves Khepri’s Fall only after the civilians do.”

Her eyes narrowed, yet the weapons display behind her remained dark. “You negotiate from a weak position.”

“For once,” I answered, “I know exactly what that feels like.”

The channel closed. I ordered the navigation crew to prepare a shuttle and told security to stand down their weapons. It was a small concession, but it was the first one I had made that did not end in gunfire. Then I sent the miners a message: the corridor would open soon, and I was going below to make certain it did.


The message to the miners had barely cleared the local network when the command room erupted into motion. Cargo manifests unfolded across the display, each one stamped with a red oxygen warning. The outpost’s reserves were not yet critical, but the damaged scrubbers were consuming emergency canisters faster than the engineers had predicted. Six hours was not a promise; it was a margin.

I left the command room before anyone could ask whether I intended to keep it.

The corridor outside smelled of hot insulation and metallic dust. Khepri’s Fall had been carved through an asteroid that never should have supported a settlement, and every passage sloped or narrowed according to the stone’s original shape. Warning strips pulsed along the floor as I moved toward the old shaft lifts. Behind the bulkheads, machinery groaned beneath the distant pressure of the blockade. The Veyr ships had not fired, but their gravity projectors tugged constantly at the outpost, making loose tools tremble in their racks.

At the lift junction, I stopped beneath a security camera and opened a channel to the flagship. “Envoy, I’m proceeding to the reliquary chamber. I want the corridor specification before I board your shuttle.”

Her face appeared in the air above the panel, pale membrane lit by transmission static. “You intend to inspect the relic before surrendering it?”

“I intend to make sure it can be moved without killing everyone in the shaft.”

“That is not your condition.”

“It is the practical part of my condition.”

For several breaths, she said nothing. Her four eyes shifted independently, measuring me in a way no human expression could imitate. Behind her, I could see the blurred silhouettes of Veyr officers and the curved architecture of the flagship’s command chamber. They had not lowered their weapons. Neither had I, though my sidearm remained locked in the command room as required.

“The medical corridor will extend from your outpost’s eastern docking ring,” she said. “One shuttle every twelve minutes. No military personnel aboard. No cargo except medical equipment and personal survival packs.”

“Civilians first.”

“Medical personnel first.”

“Civilians who need treatment cannot wait behind a classification dispute.”

Her central membrane tightened. “You bargain over categories while your oxygen fails.”

“I bargain because categories are how people get left behind.”

The sentence lingered between us. I had said something similar before Orison, though then I had used procedure as a shield. The Veyr relief vessel had ignored my challenge, and I had decided that silence meant hostile intent. Thirty-seven dead because I had mistaken uncertainty for permission. Now the envoy’s silence felt like a weapon pointed at a different part of me.

“Very well,” she said. “The first three shuttles will carry the injured and those dependent on assisted respiration. After that, civilians will be loaded by household group. You will board the fourth shuttle.”

“With the reliquary?”

“Without it, the corridor closes.”

I looked toward the lift doors. “The relic stays here until the first civilian shuttle clears the blockade.”

“That is unacceptable.”

“It is the only way I will know your promise is real.”

The envoy leaned closer to the transmission field. “Captain Vale, the Alliance remembers human promises.”

“So do I,” I said. “That is why I’m asking for one you can keep.”

The channel ended without agreement, but not with a refusal. I took that as progress because I had learned not to demand more from silence.

The lift carried me down through the oldest part of Khepri’s Fall. The walls changed from reinforced alloy to raw black stone veined with copper-colored crystal. Ancient drilling scars crossed the surfaces beneath newer support struts. As the platform descended, the outpost noise faded until I could hear only the lift cables and my own breathing.

At the bottom, a pressure door stood open. Beyond it, miners had cleared a path around the excavation, leaving the chamber crowded with floodlamps and suspended dust. I recognized the shape from the envoy’s image: a low, faceted object half-buried in the stone, no larger than a coffin but far heavier-looking than its size suggested. Its surface shifted whenever I looked away, as if the angles refused to remain fixed.

I stepped inside the marked perimeter.

The reliquary answered with a pulse of blue light.

For one instant, I smelled rain on the plains of Orison. I heard the relief vessel’s captain refusing my challenge. Then the memory fractured. The voice became my own, saying, Fire.

I stumbled backward and caught the rail.

No one in the chamber moved. The miners saw only a light, perhaps. They could not have heard what I heard. I pressed my palm against the cold rail until the false memory receded, leaving my heart hammering.

The relic had not merely shown me the past. It had edited it.

I activated the chamber intercom. “Seal this level. No one enters without my authorization. Keep the reliquary connected to the ground anchors, but isolate its power feed from the outpost grid.”

A technician’s voice answered from the control booth. “That may interrupt the stabilizers.”

“Then find a mechanical brace. We are not carrying it anywhere until the civilians are moving.”

I turned toward the lift and opened a general command channel. “All departments, begin corridor preparation. Injured and assisted-respiration cases to the eastern ring first. No one boards without a manifest. The Veyr have offered us a route, and I intend to make them honor it.”

Above me, the outpost shuddered as the blockade adjusted formation. Through the stone came a deep, slow vibration, like the growl of something enormous circling outside.

I looked once more at the reliquary. It had shown me a memory I trusted—and changed one word inside it. That was enough to make every confession suspect, including my own.

Then I entered the lift and ordered it upward, toward the docking ring, the waiting civilians, and the shuttle that would carry me unarmed into the Veyr blockade.


The lift rose through the asteroid’s spine, its cables whining whenever the blockade shifted overhead.

I kept one hand on the emergency rail and the other pressed against the command band at my wrist. The display showed three evacuation manifests assembling in the eastern ring: patients with crushed limbs, miners whose lungs depended on assisted-respiration rigs, children whose names had been marked in red by the medical staff.

No weapons. No military personnel. No exceptions.

A tremor ran through the lift.

Dust sifted from the ceiling. “Status,” I said.

The logistics officer answered through static. “First shuttle is fueled. The ring doors are sealed against the external pressure differential.

We have two hundred and eighteen passengers assigned, but the Veyr are requesting biometric confirmation before opening the corridor. ”

“Send the manifests.

”

“We did.

They claim our transponder lattice can conceal soldiers.

”

I looked at the black reflection of my own face in the lift door. Without the captain’s insignia, I looked younger than I felt. “Tell them to scan every passenger twice.

If they find a soldier, they can close the corridor on us. ”

There was a pause.

“Captain, command security wants permission to place a guard detail aboard. ”

“No military personnel on the first three shuttles. ”

“They’re worried about sabotage.

”

“So am I.

That is why no one armed boards a medical flight.

”

The lift doors opened onto the eastern transit level. The sound struck me first: coughing, machinery, the thin electronic chirps of oxygen monitors. The docking ring had been converted into a triage hall.

Families sat beneath thermal blankets while medics threaded hoses beneath collars and taped sensors to gray, frightened skin. Beyond the pressure doors, the shuttle waited with its nose pointed toward the blockade, small and absurd against the darkness outside.

I walked into the crowd, and heads turned.

Some recognized me from the command broadcast.

Others recognized the empty space on my collar. A miner with an oxygen mask caught my sleeve.

“Are they letting us out?

Then, after the evacuation preparations were complete, the protagonist rode the lift from Khepri’s Fall’s preparation sector to the eastern docking ring and authorized civilian boarding under the continuing Veyr blockade; only after boarding and launch did confirmation arrive that the first medical flight had cleared, advancing the local objective from preparation to evacuation without replaying earlier events and establishing scene progression c3s1 while preserving scene_000’s accepted outcome and evt_scene_000_01. This local replan bridge kept the disgraced young captain responsible for protecting the outpost’s civilians under the envoy’s conditional terms—the first three shuttles reserved for injured civilians and those dependent on assisted respiration, no military personnel aboard those medical shuttles, and the captain boarding the fourth shuttle unarmed only after all civilians had evacuated and transport was safe—while the memory-altering relic remained grounded on Khepri’s Fall and isolated from its grid; pending constraint progress therefore meant reserving the fourth shuttle’s onward route so the protagonist could bring the relic to the Veyr flagship after evacuation to secure the medical corridor, sustaining the fragile peace with an alliance still haunted by myths of human ferocity without treating provisional passage as a secured corridor or authorizing premature departure.

Then, after scene_001 completed the evacuation preparations, event order advances monotonically from 7 to 8: the protagonist rides the lift from Khepri’s Fall’s evacuation-preparation sector under Veyr blockade to the eastern docking ring, where he orders civilian boarding to begin, providing location transition evidence and moving the outpost into evacuation under Veyr blockade; this local replan bridge establishes scene progression c3s1 as char protagonist advances local objective while preserving the agreed conditional terms with the Veyr envoy: the first three shuttles will carry injured civilians and those dependent on assisted respiration, no military personnel will board those medical shuttles, and the protagonist will board the fourth shuttle unarmed only after civilian evacuation is complete, keeping the relic grounded and isolated from the outpost grid until then; pending constraint progress—the protagonist must bring the relic to the Veyr flagship to secure the medical corridor—therefore proceeds through evacuation first and delivery afterward, preserving scene_000 accepted and evt_scene_000_01 without reversing any earlier event. We are not leaving anyone who can be moved.

”

He searched my face as though trying to find the lie. I could not blame him. The Veyr had made promises, and I had made promises, and the relic beneath our feet had demonstrated how easily memory could turn one into the other. The docking controller waved me toward the command console.

“We have a problem.

The blockade has changed formation.

”

The main viewport brightened.

Twelve Veyr warships had become thirteen. One vessel had slid beneath the others, presenting a long silver underside toward the ring.

Its gravity projectors cast a faint distortion across the stars.

“They’re tightening the cordon,” I said. “Or aiming at us. ”

A transmission opened before I could answer.

The envoy appeared above the console, her four eyes reflecting the red evacuation lights.

Behind her, unfamiliar Veyr officers moved in rigid silence. “Captain Vale,” she said.

“Your shuttle is ready to depart when the first three manifests are verified.

”

“And the reliquary? ”

“Still beneath your outpost.

”

“Good.

”

One of the officers behind her leaned toward the envoy.

I could not hear the exchange, but the envoy’s membrane darkened.

Then she faced me again.

“The Alliance council requires proof that you intend to honor the exchange. Bring the reliquary to the fourth shuttle. You will board without weapons. Once it reaches the flagship, the medical corridor will remain open. ”

“Once the first civilian shuttle clears the blockade,” I said.

Her eyes narrowed.

“You continue to repeat that condition.

”

“Because you continue to avoid accepting it. ”

The command room behind her seemed to become very still.

I imagined the old stories sitting there with them—the human captain who never stopped advancing, the predator who called surrender a tactic.

My voice sounded calm only because I had learned what happened when I allowed fear to speak first. At last, the envoy said, “The first civilian shuttle may clear the blockade before the relic leaves Khepri’s Fall.

”

“May?

”

“That is the language I am authorized to use.

”

“Then authorize better language.

”

For a moment I expected the channel to close.

Instead, she lifted one narrow hand.

“The first shuttle will be granted passage.

If it clears the cordon without hostile action, the second and third will follow. After that, you will bring the reliquary to the fourth. ”

It was not trust.

It was a procedure with a gun behind it. But procedures could be held accountable. “I accept the sequence,” I said.

“Not the threat.

”

“Those are often the same thing to humans. ”

“Only when someone mistakes fear for certainty.

”

Her gaze lingered on me, and I wondered whether she remembered Orison as I did—or as the relic wanted me to.

Then the transmission dissolved. The first shuttle’s hatch sealed. I checked the manifest myself: injured miners, assisted-respiration patients, two medics, no security badges, no weapons.

When the pilot requested clearance, I gave it. The outer doors opened.

Vacuum swallowed the ring’s noise, and the shuttle slid into the black between the outpost and the Veyr crescent.

Every warship tracked it.

My pulse followed the tiny blue marker across the viewport.

It passed the first patrol line. A warning flashed: Veyr targeting systems active.

I gripped the console until my knuckles hurt.

The relic remained grounded below, isolated from the grid. The corridor existed only as long as the Veyr chose restraint, and restraint was a language both species mistrusted. Then the shuttle crossed the blockade and its transponder turned green. Around me, people began to breathe as if they had been holding their lungs shut. I opened the reliquary command channel.

“Prepare the fourth-shuttle transfer,” I ordered. “Keep the relic sealed and mechanically braced until the second and third flights clear.

I will board the fourth unarmed.

”

The lift doors behind me opened toward the freight access shaft.

Somewhere below, the memory-changing relic waited in the dark. Somewhere ahead, the Veyr flagship waited with its guns trained on my home. For the first time, the route between them was real.


I stopped at the freight lift and looked back at the docking controller. The first shuttle’s green marker had almost vanished beyond the blockade. Two more waited beside the departure clock, still amber.

“Preparing the fourth doesn’t authorize its launch,” I said. “No relic transfer until those two are clear. No boarding for me until the civilian count is zero.”

The controller repeated the conditions into his recorder. Only then did I step into the lift.

Descending alone, I watched the evacuation manifests scroll across my wrist. The second flight held the remaining stretcher cases. The third would take the last assisted-respiration patients, their households, and the civilian medical staff. Every available seat had a name; every gap between names represented someone who might be forgotten. I compared the lists against the outpost register until my eyes watered.

At the reliquary level, the pressure door opened onto cold stone and floodlight glare. Technicians had fitted the object into a wheeled cradle, its mechanical braces bolted through the frame. The power feed lay disconnected on the floor. A plain cargo shroud concealed the facets.

“Has anyone approached it?” I asked.

“Only to fit the braces,” a technician answered through the booth speaker. “No further light.”

That was not the same as no further effect. I stood outside the marked perimeter and checked the seals against the chamber’s recorded images. I remembered Orison’s relief captain refusing my challenge. I remembered my own voice where his should have been. Neither recollection could serve as evidence now, but the dead remained dead. Uncertainty about a memory did not absolve me of the order I had given.

My wrist chimed. The second shuttle had launched.

I opened its external camera feed. Khepri’s Fall dwindled behind it, a pocked fragment wrapped in docking spars. Beyond lay thirteen warships, their hulls bright against the stars.

An amber targeting warning covered the image.

“Maintain your assigned vector,” I told the civilian pilot.

“I am.”

“I know.”

I muted myself before fear could make me issue another unnecessary instruction.

The envoy’s channel opened beside the feed. “Your transfer vessel reports no passenger.”

“Because the evacuation is incomplete.”

“Our observers report the second flight underway.”

“Underway isn’t clear.”

Her lower eyes shifted toward something outside the image. “There are officers here who consider this delay evidence of deception.”

There it was again: a human waiting must be laying an ambush. A human bargaining must be buying time to strike.

“Then give them something observable,” I said. “Transmit the fourth shuttle’s inspection requirements. I’ll meet them here.”

“You could have prepared a weapon aboard the outpost.”

“You could destroy the outpost while we discuss it. Neither possibility tells us what is happening.”

Her membrane tightened. After a moment, an inspection checklist appeared on my display.

I laid my empty belt, command tools, and pocket cutter on the chamber bench. Under the booth camera, I turned out each pocket. The cutter made a small, ordinary sound against the metal. Surrendering it felt more intimate than leaving my sidearm behind had.

“Keep the recording,” I told the technician. “Send an identical copy to both sides.”

The envoy watched without comment.

The second shuttle’s marker turned green.

I let out a breath, then contacted the ring. “Third flight status?”

“Last passengers boarding. Habitat sweeps complete. We’re reconciling the register.”

“Tell me when it balances.”

We waited beside the covered cradle. A cooling pipe ticked overhead. Somewhere above us, a freight coupling hammered against its stops as the blockade’s gravity projectors shifted. I wanted to move, to spend that waiting on something useful. Instead I checked the seals again.

The third flight launched with the last civilian medic aboard. The controller sent the reconciled register, followed by sweep confirmations for the habitation levels and mine shelters. No civilians remained on Khepri’s Fall. I read the report twice, but left the cradle’s wheel locks engaged until the shuttle crossed the outer patrol line.

Its marker turned green.

“Evacuation complete,” I said into the shared channel. “Request safe clearance for the fourth shuttle.”

The envoy supplied a route and a matching cease-targeting acknowledgment. I required the fourth shuttle’s pilot to confirm both before I released the locks.

I pushed the cradle into the freight lift myself.

At the eastern ring, empty blankets lay beneath the benches. The silence hurt more than the coughing had. The Veyr pilot scanned me at the hatch, then scanned the sealed cradle. I stood with my hands open until the instrument lowered.

Only after the relic was secured did I board.

The shuttle detached from Khepri’s Fall and carried us between the waiting guns. I kept the evacuation markers visible throughout the crossing. Their passage remained provisional; delivering the reliquary was the price of keeping the medical route open.

When the flagship’s receiving clamps closed around us, I rose too quickly and caught the restraint across my knees.

Beyond the hatch waited an inspection chamber and two armed Veyr.

I unfastened the cradle from its deck mount. The relic had reached their flagship after my civilians had reached safety. Now I had to make sure the bargain survived the opening of a door.


The receiving bay smelled of hot metal and antiseptic vapor. Beyond the open hatch, the Veyr flagship rose in tiers of dark alloy, its walls ribbed like the inside of a shell. Two armed guards stood beside the inspection threshold, rifles lowered but ready. I kept both hands visible and guided the cradle across the painted line.

“Stop there,” one of them ordered.

I stopped. The cradle’s wheels clicked once and settled.

The envoy entered from a side passage, flanked by a recording drone. She wore no armor, but the officers behind her did. Her gaze moved from my empty hands to the sealed shroud, then to the shuttle hatch through which we had arrived.

“Your civilian flights have cleared,” she said.

“All three,” I replied. “The fourth carried me and the reliquary only after the last medical marker crossed your outer patrol line. The registers, habitat sweeps, and targeting acknowledgments are duplicated in the transfer record.”

“I have seen the record.”

“Then you know what I am asking.”

“Continued access to the medical corridor.”

“Not access,” I said. “Protection. Your patrols must hold the route open while Khepri’s Fall receives oxygen cartridges and evacuation support. The outpost is still under your blockade. The people we moved are safe for the moment, but the ones remaining to repair the habitat cannot survive if your ships treat every cargo vessel as an attack.”

One of the armored officers shifted his rifle. His helmet speaker clicked on. “The human captain delivered an object capable of compromising memory. That is not proof of peaceful intent.”

“No,” I said. “It is proof that I kept my word.”

The envoy’s lower eyes narrowed. “You understand why the Alliance fears this device.”

“I understand why you fear what you believe it did.”

A silence spread through the bay. The old human legends had reached even this flagship: stories of captains who burned surrendering ships, soldiers who turned negotiation into bait, entire worlds supposedly conquered by fleets that never offered terms. The Veyr saw those stories whenever I asked for trust. I had learned not to demand that they forget them. I had to give them better evidence than a denial.

I reached toward the cradle, then stopped short of touching it. “Inspection begins with an inventory. No one opens the reliquary. No one connects it to your systems. We document its condition, its power state, and every person within the chamber. If you want a second inspection team, choose one from your officers and one from my outpost’s medical administration. Both teams observe the same procedure.”

The envoy glanced at the drone. “And if the object has already altered your memory?”

“Then record my statement before you decide whether to believe it.”

“That is not a safeguard.”

“It is an admission of uncertainty. Your officers keep calling uncertainty deception because the alternative would require them to admit they do not know what the human mind is doing.”

The words struck harder than I intended. The armed officer raised his rifle a fraction. I did not move. The envoy lifted one hand, and the weapon lowered again.

She approached the cradle. A scanner unfolded from her wrist and passed over the shroud without touching it. Blue light mapped the braces, the bolts, and the disconnected power feed. Nothing answered from beneath the covering.

“Remove the shroud,” she said.

I looked at the recording drone. “State that the first visual exposure is authorized and witnessed.”

The envoy repeated the authorization. I pulled the release tabs. The shroud slid away, revealing the reliquary’s black facets, each one reflecting the bay lights without returning them. The object seemed smaller than it had in the chamber beneath Khepri’s Fall. That made it more dangerous, not less. Something that could fit beneath a coat could enter a room unnoticed.

The scanner swept across it again. One facet brightened.

Only once. A thin pulse of amber crossed the cradle and vanished.

The guards snapped their rifles up.

“Hold,” I said.

The envoy’s eyes fixed on the relic. “You said it was unpowered.”

“It is disconnected.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No,” I said, feeling the old uncertainty open beneath my ribs. “It isn’t.”

For a moment, the bay’s walls seemed to tilt. I remembered Orison’s command deck, the red emergency lighting, my own order to fire. Then the memory broke apart under scrutiny: a voice without a face, a hand on a console I could not place. I forced myself to look at the present—the sealed braces, the envoy’s raised hand, the rifles aimed at the floor rather than my chest.

“Record the pulse,” I said. “Do not erase it, and do not let the relic explain it for you.”

The envoy studied me instead of the object. “You believe it manipulates memory.”

“I believe it can. I also believe fear will make every unexplained event look like an attack.”

“And what do you propose?”

“A quarantine chamber with no network access. Mechanical observation only. Your technicians may inspect the casing. My people may verify that the outpost’s systems remain untouched. While that happens, you issue a written corridor order covering the next medical convoy.”

“That is a demand.”

“It is the bargain’s next step.”

The envoy considered the relic, then the evacuation record hovering beside the cradle. At last she turned to the nearest officer. “Seal Chamber Seven. No neural interface, no tactical uplink, no personnel without paired observers.”

The officer hesitated. “Envoy—”

“Do it.”

The guards lowered their rifles, though neither released his grip. I took hold of the cradle’s handle and began pushing toward the marked passage. The envoy walked beside me, close enough to speak without the drone amplifying us.

“This does not secure your corridor,” she said.

“I know.”

“It secures only the inspection.”

“Then we have something real to negotiate from.”

Behind us, the receiving bay doors sealed against the black. Ahead, Chamber Seven opened beneath sterile white lights. I guided the relic across the threshold, carrying the bargain farther into the flagship without pretending it had become trust.


The envoy entered last, and the recording drone floated through the closing seam before Chamber Seven sealed behind us with a pressure-heavy thud. The sound traveled through the deck and into my teeth. I kept one hand on the cradle while the guards took positions at either side of the door. Their rifles remained lowered, but the muzzles followed every movement I made. The chamber’s isolation field came alive.

A red line appeared across the floor.

“Behind it,” the envoy said.

I moved the cradle into the marked square and stepped back behind the line. “Confirm the medical flights remain protected while this inspection proceeds.”

“Your second and third flights cleared the patrol perimeter,” she replied. “The corridor is still open.”

“Open is not protected.”

Her gaze sharpened. “You have a talent for making concessions sound like failures.”

“I have a talent for recognizing the difference. At Khepri’s Fall, a route that was merely open could still be closed by a nervous gunner.”

The drone projected a copy of the evacuation record into the air. Three green flight markers moved across the display, their routes preserved in parallel lines. Beneath them, the fourth shuttle’s passenger and cargo manifest showed only my name and the reliquary’s sealed cargo designation. I watched the record stabilize, grateful for the evidence and suspicious of my relief. The reliquary had crossed to the flagship only after the second and third medical flights cleared. That sequence mattered. If the Veyr chose to doubt everything else, they could not honestly doubt that.

The envoy touched two fingers to her wrist. A document appeared between us, rendered in the Veyr script and translated beneath it.

“Provisional corridor order,” she said. “The next medical convoy may approach Khepri’s Fall under escort. No weapons discharge against marked medical craft unless the craft alters its declared vector or emits a weapons signature.”

“Who can revoke it?”

“Only the Alliance watch commander assigned to the blockade.”

“Then the watch commander needs a copy that cannot be revised by a tactical uplink.”

A guard’s helmet turned toward me. “You are demanding control of our orders?”

“I am demanding that the pilots receive the same order you just showed me.”

The envoy studied my face, or perhaps the scars beside it. “You assume our officers will obey a human captain’s interpretation.”

“I assume they will obey a document signed by their envoy. That is why I am asking for your signature, not mine.”

For several breaths, only the chamber’s ventilation answered. Then she altered the document. A seal formed at its base, a branching mark like a split wing. The drone queued copies for the outpost command room, the medical coordinators, and the fourth shuttle’s flight console. The corridor order was not peace. It was a narrow permission to keep people alive, and for the moment that was enough to make the next negotiation possible.

I turned back to the reliquary. Its black facets held the chamber lights without reflecting the guards or the envoy. The amber pulse from the receiving bay had not repeated. I pointed to the scanner resting on its mechanical arm.

“Run the same sweep again,” I said. “No neural interface. No network. Record every interval.”

The envoy nodded to one of the guards, who activated the scanner from a manual control panel. A pale grid passed over the casing. The readings appeared on a separate screen: no external power, no radio emission, no thermal increase. Yet one interior facet returned a faint residual pattern, not energy exactly, but a sequence of changed values.

The envoy leaned toward the display. “It responded to the scanner.”

“Or the scanner exposed a stored response.”

“You said it could manipulate memory.”

“I said I believe it can. The pulse alone does not prove that.”

“Your own memory is disputed.”

The accusation landed cleanly because I had carried it here myself. Orison’s command deck rose behind my eyes—the red lights, the order to fire, the certainty that I had heard the relief captain authorize engagement. Then the image lost its edges. I could not tell whether the relic had touched that memory or whether guilt had worn it smooth over the years.

“I will not use an uncertain memory as evidence against your people,” I said. “Do not use one as evidence against mine.”

The envoy looked from me to the dark object. “And what will you use?”

“The record. Independent observers. Repeated tests. Anything that survives being witnessed by people who want different answers.”

That seemed to trouble her more than a threat would have. She ordered the scanner stopped and had the readings printed onto sealed polymer strips. I signed the human chain-of-custody panel, then watched her add the Veyr seal beside mine. The relic remained isolated. Its pulse remained unexplained. But the inspection had produced something neither side could erase without leaving proof.

Outside Chamber Seven, the blockade still surrounded Khepri’s Fall, and the medical corridor would depend on a document traveling through hostile hands. I rested my palm against the cradle’s handle.

“Next,” I said, “we test whether the order reaches the outpost before the convoy launches.”

The envoy did not promise success. She opened the communications panel herself to transmit the queued copies, and together we waited until the first acknowledgment from Khepri’s Fall confirmed receipt before launch.


The acknowledgment from Khepri’s Fall remained on the panel long enough for me to read it twice. Order received. Launch held pending escort confirmation. Beneath the text, the outpost controller had attached the convoy’s cargo manifest: oxygen cartridges, surgical packs, replacement seals for the failing habitat locks. No weapons. No passengers on the inbound leg. I pressed my thumb against the edge of the printed corridor order until the polymer bent.

“The outpost has it,” I said. “Does the watch commander?”

“The transmission was addressed to both.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

The envoy closed the panel with a sharp movement. For an instant I thought I had spent the last of her patience. Then she faced the guards. “Chamber Seven remains sealed after we leave. No further scans. Record any visible change without approaching the cradle.”

I looked at the reliquary. Nothing moved within its black facets. The residual pattern existed on our jointly sealed strips, but I still could not say what it meant. “Paired observers,” I reminded her.

“They remain here.”

One guard stayed beside the manual recording apparatus; another took position at the threshold. The envoy opened the door, and I followed her across the isolation line, carrying my copy of the inspection record. We passed through a short pressure vestibule into a narrow passage. A third guard joined us there, rifle resting across his chest. Behind us, Chamber Seven’s locks engaged in sequence.

The communications gallery lay one deck above. We climbed a curved stair whose steps were too shallow for my boots, then entered beneath a display of the blockade. Khepri’s Fall hung at its center, a scarred lump of ore surrounded by ship markers. The medical approach was a thin white line through overlapping weapons envelopes. Seeing it at this scale made my stomach tighten. A pilot could hold the assigned vector perfectly and still spend the entire approach inside firing range.

The envoy led me to a terminal separated from the main stations by a transparent partition. “You may witness communications here. You may not address tactical personnel without authorization.”

“Then ask for acknowledgment of the signed order.”

She entered the request. An answer appeared almost immediately.

RECEIVED. IMPLEMENTATION SUBJECT TO WATCH REVIEW.

I let out a breath through my nose. “That isn’t escort confirmation.”

“It is not refusal either.”

“Tell the convoy to keep holding.”

She looked at me before relaying it. I hated giving that instruction. Every delay cost air at the outpost, but launching into an argument between Alliance officers would make the freighters hostages to our paperwork.

A voice sounded from the terminal, clipped by translation. “The manifest lists mining-rated pressure vessels.”

“Oxygen cartridges,” I said.

The envoy raised one finger toward me. “Watch commander, identify the discrepancy.”

“Such vessels can conceal fragmentation charges. Human vessels have previously used civilian declarations to close engagement distance.”

The guard behind me shifted his feet. I kept my hands on the terminal ledge. Somewhere in the Alliance’s histories there would be a real incident underneath that warning. Somewhere else, a retelling would have made every human freighter into the same ship.

“May I answer?” I asked.

The envoy opened my channel.

“Compare the cartridge serials with the depot’s dispatch record. The convoy can transmit both without leaving its holding position.”

“Records can be falsified.”

“Yes. What inspection would satisfy you without requiring the freighters to cross your guns first?”

The terminal remained quiet. On the display, an escort marker moved away from the corridor’s outer end. I watched it, trying not to imagine a targeting officer doing the same calculations.

“You are the captain censured at Orison,” the commander said.

My collar felt suddenly tight. I was younger than most of the officers in this gallery, and my disgrace had traveled farther than any commendation ever had.

“Yes.”

“Then you understand our caution.”

“I understand why you want evidence. You have my censure in front of you. Give the cargo records the same attention.”

The envoy’s lower eyes turned toward me. She did not interrupt.

The commander requested the depot seals, container masses, and an external image of each rack. I relayed the requirements through the authorized channel, then waited while the convoy crews worked. The first images arrived with gloved hands still visible beside the serial plates. I checked each number against the manifest as the envoy checked the Alliance translation. One blurred digit required another photograph. No one called it sabotage.

At last, the terminal sounded again.

“Escort assigned to the outer inspection point. Engines and weapons emissions will be monitored. Passage remains revocable by this watch.”

“Read back the signed non-engagement conditions,” the envoy said.

The commander did. I followed every clause on my polymer copy.

Only then did I authorize the convoy to leave its hold. On the blockade display, the first freighter’s marker edged toward the white line. The envoy saved the acknowledgment beside our corridor order and placed her seal on the record.

I set my copy beside hers, keeping the approaching freighter in view. It had permission, an assigned escort, and a commander who had repeated the conditions aloud. It had not yet crossed a single gun.


The first freighter advanced three ship lengths before its marker turned amber.

I gripped the terminal ledge. Beside the corridor order, a new line appeared: DRIVE VARIANCE—ASSESSMENT PENDING. The escort slid across the freighter’s projected course, placing itself between the convoy and Khepri’s Fall. Nothing fired. On the larger display, though, two overlapping weapons envelopes brightened around the medical approach.

“Keep my channel open?” I asked.

The envoy touched the authorization field. “For this exchange.”

“Convoy lead, report the variance. No compensating burn until the escort acknowledges.”

The reply arrived through a hiss of interference. “Port maneuvering assembly is cold. Automatic trim requested additional thrust. We rejected it. Holding present output.”

I looked at the freighter’s telemetry. Its heading remained inside the permitted band, but the plot showed a slow drift toward the edge. Holding output would not keep it there indefinitely.

The watch commander spoke before I could ask. “Additional thrust could conceal a rapid approach.”

“It could,” I said. “What correction will you authorize?”

“Maintain current output pending assessment.”

At Orison, I had mistaken urgency for permission. I could still feel the command chair’s restraint against my ribs. Here, every instinct demanded that I tell the pilot to correct the drift and argue afterward. I flattened my hands on the ledge.

“Then record the drift rate,” I said. “The ship is complying. It must not be classified as a deliberate deviation while it obeys your hold.”

The envoy leaned closer to the screen. “Commander, acknowledge that distinction.”

A pause followed. “Recorded. Current deviation is not classified as hostile.”

Behind the partition, an officer pointed toward a recessed station below the main display. The envoy followed the gesture, then turned to me. “The inspection telemetry is clearer at the liaison console. You will remain separated from tactical controls.”

She opened the gallery’s side gate. I took my polymer records and followed her down the short ramp into the liaison alcove, with the guard one pace behind. From here, the blockade display rose above us like a ceiling. The local console showed the freighter’s actual attitude rather than the simplified marker: a blunt cargo hull, frost along one flank, correction jets dark.

The envoy transferred our authorized connection. I waited for its green border before speaking.

“Convoy lead, transmit the maneuvering assembly maintenance entry and the temperature reading. Passive instruments only.”

“You suspect a fault?” the commander asked.

“I suspect we should compare the warning with something other than a story about human freighters.”

The envoy’s fingers stopped above the console.

I heard how it had sounded. “The history may be accurate,” I added. “This ship still needs its own assessment.”

The commander did not answer, but the request remained open.

The maintenance entry arrived with a depot timestamp and a warning the pilot had acknowledged before departure: reduced cold-start efficiency, starboard correction preferred. I put it beside the engine trace. The port assembly’s temperature matched the warning. No weapons emissions appeared on either the convoy’s record or the escort’s independent feed.

“Send those together,” I told the envoy.

She checked the identifiers before attaching her seal. I added mine. Neither signature made the machinery safe; they established which evidence we had actually examined.

“Starboard correction only,” the commander said at last. “One pulse, within the transmitted limit. Escort will match.”

The pilot read back the limit. I watched the numbers climb, stop, and settle. On the overhead display, the freighter’s path bent gently toward the corridor center. The escort moved with it. The bright weapons envelopes remained, but no longer tightened.

Only then did I notice the ache in my jaw.

“Correction complete,” the pilot reported.

“Received,” the commander said. “Proceed to outer inspection point. No clearance beyond that point is implied.”

I saved the exchange before another message could displace it.

The envoy watched me copy the record. “You expected the commander to treat it as a threat.”

“I expected someone to call obedience a threat.”

“And you believe the distinction is now settled?”

“For that correction. Not for the next one.”

She placed her seal beneath the saved instruction without offering agreement.

At the edge of my records lay the sealed strip from Chamber Seven. The reliquary’s residual pattern showed faintly through its cover. I turned it facedown. Whatever the secret machine could do to memory, it had no place in proving what this pilot had just done. The chamber remained sealed under paired observation; I would not ask anyone to approach it while frightened crews waited beneath guns.

The freighter reached the outer inspection point. Its marker stopped beside the escort, still amber. The second vessel waited farther out, engines steady, carrying habitat seals that Khepri’s Fall could not manufacture.

I requested acknowledgment of the completed correction and inspection arrival. The commander supplied both. The envoy authenticated them beside our original order.

We had made one part of the corridor work. No one had yet been allowed through.

“Now,” I said, keeping my voice level, “please give the pilot the inspection sequence before you ask the pilot to move again.”

The envoy entered the request herself. Above us, the escort’s inspection lights came on.


The inspection lights came on in sequence, washing the freighter’s hull in pale bands. They revealed every dent, patch, and frozen seam. Through the liaison console, the escort’s cameras fed us three angles at once: cargo spine, engine housing, and docking collar. The ship looked less like a weapon than a tired animal being examined under bright lamps.

“Inspection sequence transmitted,” the envoy said. “The pilot has acknowledged receipt.”

I read the order from the shared screen. Engines at idle. Weapons safed and externally verified. Cargo images first, then pressure-seal readings, then a paired boarding team only if the watch accepted the remote evidence. No movement beyond the outer point without a separate clearance.

“Add the final restriction,” I said. “No attitude adjustment during inspection unless the escort orders it.”

The envoy glanced at me. “That is already implied.”

“Implied conditions become accusations when something twitches.”

She entered the amendment rather than arguing. Her seal appeared beside mine, followed by the watch commander’s acknowledgment. I saved the record to the convoy file and sent a copy to Khepri’s Fall’s command room. The outpost had been waiting for the oxygen cartridges, but waiting did not mean we could let a frightened crew improvise inside a weapons envelope.

A sharp tone sounded from the inspection feed. One of the freighter’s external cargo cameras had lost focus. Its view blurred across the central panel, turning the containers into pale blocks. At the same instant, the escort marker flashed amber.

“Camera fault,” the pilot reported. “Request permission to cycle the external mount.”

“Denied,” the commander answered.

I looked at the pressure readings. The cargo spine remained sealed. The escort’s images showed no change in the ship’s attitude, but the Alliance officers were already watching the lost feed as if it were a hand reaching for a concealed switch.

“Can the camera be reset from the inspection console?” I asked.

“Negative. Manual access only.”

The commander’s channel opened. “Manual access would require movement.”

“Then hold the vessel where it is,” I said. “Use the escort’s thermal feed to verify the spine while the pilot keeps the camera untouched.”

“Thermal resolution is insufficient to confirm container seals.”

“Insufficient is not the same as hostile. We have two independent pressure readings and the external mass profile. Ask for a second angle from the escort before you ask the freighter to move.”

The envoy repeated my request through the authorized channel. Her voice remained even, procedural, but I could hear the strain in the pauses between translated phrases. The Alliance had built its blockade around a legend: humans approached under flags of aid, then opened hidden compartments and turned civilian proximity into slaughter. Every pause in their evidence became another page in that legend.

The escort’s second camera swept across the freighter. Its thermal outline showed the cargo spine intact, with no heat blooms behind the containers. The watch commander requested the convoy’s passive pressure telemetry and compared it against the escort’s instruments. I watched the figures populate line by line. They matched within the expected tolerance.

“Record the camera failure as equipment-related,” I said. “No corrective maneuver authorized.”

The commander answered after a long silence. “Recorded provisionally.”

“Provisional records still need a basis.”

The envoy’s gaze settled on me. “You are pressing him.”

“I am making sure the record says why the ship remains under watch.”

“And if he refuses?”

“Then the refusal goes in beside the evidence.”

She did not smile, but she authenticated the exchange.

The escort’s inspection beam shifted to the docking collar. Frost feathered the outer ring. A seal indicator showed green, then flickered yellow. My pulse kicked hard enough to make the console edge tremble beneath my hand.

“Pressure fluctuation at the collar,” the commander said.

“Pilot, report.”

“Thermal contraction in the outer gasket. Internal pressure stable. We can compensate with a quarter-degree rotation.”

“No,” I said.

The word escaped before authorization. The guard behind me lifted his rifle, and the envoy’s hand stopped above the channel control.

I forced myself to breathe. “Correction: no movement without watch approval. Transmit the internal and external pressure traces. The escort can compare them.”

The commander came back immediately. “You issued an unauthorized order.”

“I withdrew it before the pilot acted.”

“That distinction is familiar to officers who have already violated engagement limits.”

The reference to Orison struck cleanly. I kept my eyes on the telemetry instead of the guard.

“Yes,” I said. “That is why I withdrew it.”

For several seconds, no one spoke. Then the envoy opened the formal response channel. “Watch commander, the captain’s statement is not a maneuver authorization. The vessel remains stationary. Please assess the requested evidence.”

The commander accepted the clarification without apology. The freighter transmitted its traces. The collar’s pressure had shifted by less than the safety margin, and the escort’s instruments showed the same change. A maintenance note identified the gasket as one of the seals replaced before departure.

I attached the note to the inspection packet. The envoy checked the translation, then placed her seal beside mine. Jointly authenticated evidence accumulated in small, stubborn pieces: the acknowledged hold, the engine fault, the authorized correction, the camera failure, the stable pressure readings. None of it erased the myths haunting the blockade. It gave the myths less room to speak.

“Inspection may proceed to cargo verification,” the commander said. “The convoy remains stationary.”

Only then did I straighten. The liaison alcove’s side hatch opened onto the receiving-bay observation corridor, and the envoy gestured toward it. I took my records and crossed the threshold with her and the armed guard, the open hatch and the active inspection feed marking the transition from communications oversight to remote cargo verification. On the corridor display, the freighter waited at the outer inspection point, still barred from Khepri’s Fall.

At the corridor console, I requested the first container image. The pilot sent it. Oxygen cartridges filled the frame, serial plates clear, seals unbroken.

“Log the image,” I said. “Then request the next rack. No movement yet.”

The envoy authenticated the record. Above us, the blockade ships held their positions, and the outpost’s dwindling air remained the reason every careful second mattered.


The next rack image arrived distorted by static. I enlarged it without touching the freighter’s controls. Six cartridges appeared behind the blur, their serial plates partly hidden by a restraint bar. The inspection software marked two seals as unreadable, and the escort’s amber indicator brightened again.

“Do not classify the unreadable plates as a discrepancy yet,” I said. “Request the same rack from the escort’s forward camera.”

The envoy routed the request through the signed corridor order. Her hands moved quickly over the console, but she kept her body angled so I could see every command before it left the station. The armed guard remained behind us, rifle held across his chest. I felt the weapon’s presence without looking back. It was a reminder that cooperation had not become trust, and that my first mistake at Orison still occupied more space in the Alliance’s judgment than the evidence accumulating here.

The forward camera answered with a sharper image. The plates were not concealed; the restraint bar had been mounted across them at an awkward angle. The serials matched the cargo manifest, and the seal patterns matched the manufacturer’s record transmitted before approach.

“Cross-reference the manifest,” I said.

“Already doing so,” the envoy replied.

A tone sounded from the overhead display. The watch commander’s channel opened, carrying the translated voice over a background of clipped alerts. “The forward camera confirms the plates. Rack one is accepted. Continue.”

The display labeled his source as BLOCKADE CONTROL—INNER WATCH. It was the first clear location attached to his voice since the inspection began. I saved the designation with his acknowledgment. Somewhere beyond the corridor’s armored walls, he was watching Khepri’s Fall through the blockade’s command net, not speaking from the freighter or from any station aboard our ship. The distinction mattered. A commander who could see the whole weapons envelope might judge caution differently from a pilot trapped inside a failing camera feed.

“Rack two,” I requested.

The pilot transmitted another image. This one showed oxygen cartridges packed in three layers, the nearest row sealed and the rear rows obscured by frost. The temperature reading sat below the preferred range but above the cargo’s transport limit. I compared it with the escort’s thermal scan. The figures disagreed by a narrow margin.

“Hold acceptance,” the commander said.

I looked at the two readings. “The escort’s sensor is reading the container surface. The freighter’s probe is internal to the rack housing. Ask for the probe calibration record and a third thermal pass.”

The envoy sent both requests. “Commander, the evidence is incomplete, not contradictory.”

“Your captain has a history of treating that distinction as permission to act.”

The guard shifted. I heard the scrape of his boot against the deck.

I turned toward the channel display. “And I have a history of acting before the distinction is recorded. I am not doing that here. No movement has been requested. No movement will occur unless your watch authorizes it.”

Silence pressed against the corridor. Beyond the observation glass, the freighter’s navigation lights remained fixed against the black. The blockade cruisers held their positions around Khepri’s Fall, a ring of restrained force between a mining outpost and the oxygen it needed. If the commander called the discrepancy hostile, the convoy would remain outside. If he ordered a boarding too soon, one frightened gesture could turn inspection into the story the Alliance had inherited about humanity.

The calibration record arrived first. The probe had been certified before departure, but its last reading had been taken against an empty housing. I attached the document to the cargo packet and marked the limitation. The third thermal pass followed, sweeping slowly across the rack. Its reading fell between the other two, close enough to confirm the cartridges remained within transport tolerance.

“Record the variance and its basis,” I said. “Rack two accepted provisionally pending physical confirmation. The cargo stays aboard until the full remote sequence is complete.”

The commander did not immediately answer. Instead, a second overlay appeared on the display: the reliquary chamber’s isolation status, pulled from the outpost’s sealed systems. CHAMBER SEVEN—NO ACCESS. The mnemonic relic remained under paired observation below Khepri’s Fall, its secret untouched while we argued over oxygen seals. I felt an old pressure behind my eyes, a flicker of uncertainty about which memories belonged to me and which might have been placed there. I shut the overlay before it could become an excuse to doubt the readings in front of me.

The envoy noticed the change. “You want the chamber status excluded from the cargo record?”

“I want nothing from Chamber Seven used to interpret this inspection.”

She studied me for a moment, then entered the exclusion note. “Agreed. Evidence must remain attached to the event that produced it.”

Her seal appeared beside mine. The commander’s acknowledgment followed, less promptly but unmistakably. “Remote verification continues. No hostile classification. Send rack three.”

I released the next request. On the overhead display, the freighter’s third rack appeared: cartridges, seals, serials, all waiting to be compared. The convoy had not advanced, the escort had not tightened its weapons envelope, and Khepri’s Fall still had a corridor—narrow, conditional, but real.

I copied the commander’s location and acknowledgment into the inspection file, then leaned toward the console.

“Rack three,” I said. “Begin with the left restraint bar.”

prompt: Imagine a story about a young London student entrusted with writing a message to launch into space, destined to return eight million years later. Show how conflicts flare when visionaries are dismissed, and weave in themes of human folly, hope, and redemption as a global power rises.

chapters.text:
London arrived at the university observatory with rain in her shoes and a summons folded inside her overdue electricity bill. She had expected an accusation about her scholarship application. Instead, Professor Show opened the door carrying a kettle with no lid.

“Mind the cable,” he said.

She stepped over an orange extension lead. Beyond him, beneath the observatory’s shuttered dome, a metal sphere rested in a cradle of white foam. It was smaller than the washing machine she shared with six other students. Someone had stuck a handwritten notice on it: NOT A BIN.

“That,” Show said, “is why you’re here.”

London kept her coat on. “Have I damaged it?”

“Not yet.”

He put the kettle beside two cups and offered her a chair whose stuffing showed through its split seat. Through the high windows she could see the river, brown and swollen between its walls. On the opposite embankment, a screen displayed the blue sunburst of the Meridian Union. Beneath it, cargo ships moved through an animation of open sea. The Union had begun by rebuilding drowned ports; now its loans paid for half the city’s flood defences, and its emblem appeared even on her scholarship letters.

Show tapped the sphere with one fingernail.

“A prototype housing. The flight vessel leaves on a long solar orbit, with stellar encounters accounted for and correction systems designed to sleep between adjustments. Its homecoming is eight million years away.”

She waited for him to smile.

“Years?”

“Yes.”

“Will there still be a London?”

“Almost certainly not.”

Her own name sounded suddenly absurd: a borrowed city she might outlast by seventy years, attached to a student who had missed breakfast.

Show handed her a thin folder. Inside was a commission bearing the university seal and the Union sunburst.

“We need a message,” he said. “Something engraved, redundant, with a decoding primer. The technical teams handle the primer. You write what we say.”

London read the first line twice. “I study literature.”

“We have sufficient engineers.”

“You have poets. Famous ones.”

“We invited them. Most submitted statements about the generosity of the sponsors.”

“And you want a cheaper statement?”

Show’s hand stopped above the cups. He set one down without pouring.

“I read your essay about the evacuation memorial.”

Her stomach tightened. The essay had cost her a departmental prize. She had written that the bronze rescuers all had faces, while the people they carried were smooth-headed bundles.

“I was told it was ungrateful.”

“You wrote that gratitude becomes dishonest when it forbids grief.”

“Is that why you chose me?”

“Yes.”

From behind a partition came the scrape of a chair. London had assumed they were alone. A man wearing a visitor’s badge emerged, fastening his coat.

“This is precisely the problem,” he said. “You confuse a communications project with a confessional.”

Show’s shoulders stiffened. “We haven’t finished.”

“The launch council has. Nobody funds a monument to human inadequacy.”

London looked down at the commission. A paragraph near the bottom required approval from the Union’s Cultural Secretariat.

“You haven’t actually entrusted me with anything,” she said. “You’ve invited me to audition.”

The visitor gave her a small, almost relieved smile. “A sensible distinction.”

Show took the folder from her, found the paragraph, and drew a line through it.

The man’s smile vanished. “You cannot amend that.”

“I control the university’s contribution.”

“You control a workshop with a leaking roof. The council gave your impossible clockwork a purpose. Try not to mistake indulgence for respect.”

London heard the rain ticking into a bucket behind the partition. Show stood very still.

Then he said, “You called the flood models impossible too.”

The visitor pulled his sleeve straight. “And now the Union builds the barriers. Some of us learned to be practical.”

He left before London could decide whether that was an answer.

Show poured the water. Most of it reached the cups.

“Did they dismiss your models?” she asked.

“Several governments did. The Union bought them later.”

“So they saved your work.”

“Yes.” He pushed a cup towards her. “That doesn’t entitle them to every word you write.”

London studied the crossed-out clause. The Union’s barriers protected her mother’s flat. Its repayment terms had closed the public library where her mother used to work. She could not make either fact cancel the other.

“If I accept,” she said, “I want your amendment countersigned before I give you a draft.”

Show nodded.

“And I want to see the decoding plan. There’s no point writing beautifully to someone who can’t read it.”

For the first time, he smiled. “That can be arranged.”

She took off her wet coat and pulled her notebook from her bag. Show cleared a space beside the sphere, moving washers, a screwdriver, and a plate containing one hardened biscuit.

London wrote: *We were here.*

She stared at it, then crossed it out. It sounded like something scratched into a desk.

Below it she tried again.

*We damaged things we loved. Some of us tried to mend them.*

Show read over her shoulder.

“Some?” he asked.

She held out the pen. “You’re allowed to argue. You’re not allowed to improve our record.”

He left the pen in her hand and sat down beside her.


Show kept his hands on his knees. He had wanted to question the word *some* because it sounded like an acquittal for everyone else, but London’s answer had caught him in a familiar habit: correcting the smallest available thing when the larger thing frightened him. Across the table lay his signature beside a cancellation he had no certainty the council would honour. He could still hear the visitor calling his work impossible clockwork.
